title.raw: Skeletal Traction: Procedure, Uses, and Recovery Plan
title.rendered: Skeletal Traction: Procedure, Uses, and Recovery Plan

content.raw:
Treating severe fractures can be complex, painful, and difficult to manage. In situations where traditional casting or splinting does not work, doctors opt for the skeletal traction technique. This method has been saving limbs for decades and is considered one of the most effective external stabilization methods. Now you might be wondering what skeletal traction is? and why is it critical to understand its procedure, its uses and recovery plan? Whether you're a patient waiting for skeletal traction treatment or a caregiver knowing all the details of this treatment might assist in reducing anxiety and having clear communication with the medical provider. In this guide, we’ll walk you through everything you need to understand about skeletal traction, whether it's the procedure, its uses or how does the recovery plan of this treatment work?

What is Skeletal Traction?

Skeletal traction is an orthopedic procedure that is used to treat complex fractures and joint-related problems. It is done by applying a steady pulling force directly to the bone. This treatment is done by inserting pins, wires, or screws into the fractured bone through surgery. The weight applied during the procedure depends upon the patient's body weight or injury type, typically ranging between 10-20 pounds(7kg).

Bones Where Skeletal Traction Is Most Effective?

  • Distal femur
  • Proximal tibia
  • Cervical spine

Skeletal Traction Procedure

The skeletal traction procedure is done quite carefully under controlled medical examination. This is because this surgery is done by directly applying continuous pressure on the bone. The skeletal traction procedure comprises the following steps:
  • Pre-Procedure Preparation
Comprehensive diagnostic imaging is done to determine the exact location and severity of the fracture.
  • Pin or Wire insertion
A metal surgical Steinmann pin or Kirschner wire (K-wire) is inserted into the distal femur or proximal tibia.
  • Weight and Pulley Application
With the help of pulleys, weights of around 7kg or more is attached to the pin inserter. This is the step where constant tension is applied to the affected bone.
  • Post-procedure Monitoring
The patient is monitored for blood circulation, infection due to pin insertion, and pain management.
  • Traction Maintenance
The force is applied again until the surgery is completed. Balanced skeletal traction technique and closed reduction is used to ensure there are no skeletal traction complications.

Types of Skeletal Traction

Skeletal traction procedures have different types. The most effective type is selected based on the injury. Since this surgical procedure is applied in complex cases, it is significant to understand its type so that further complications are avoided and recovery speed increases.

Balanced Skeletal Traction

In this type of procedure, the counterweights and pulleys are used for patients' mobility and dynamic adjustment.

Femoral Skeletal Traction

This type is used for mid-thigh fractures and is applied through the femur.

Tibial Skeletal Traction

This type is preferred for lower leg injuries and is applied through the tibia.

Skeletal Traction vs Skin Traction

Although Skeletal traction and skin traction are both orthopedic surgeries but their use and application differ.

Short Comparison Table of skeletal traction and skin traction

Point Skeletal Infection Skin Traction
Surgery Application Pins and wires are inserted into the bones. Adhesive straps or bandages are applied to the skin.
Weights Used Weighs around 7kg or more Weights under 5kg
Complications More complicated due to a pin infection. Lower complications, but skin irritation.
Nursing Care Skeletal traction nursing care is required regularly. Regular care is not required
Preferred Use Cases Complex fractures, such as closed reduction. Minor hip dislocations or pediatric fractures.

Skeletal Traction Complications

Skeletal traction is an effective treatment but it needs to be handled with care as it gives tension due to weights on the bone. By understanding the skeletal traction complications the healthcare providers and caretakers can reduce the chances of risks and improve recovery. Here are a few complications:
  • Pin site infections are caused by to insertion of pins.
  • Skin breakdown due to pressure on Ulcers
  • Muscle atrophy due to extended periods in traction causes joint stiffness.
  • Malalignment occurs if the weight is not properly calibrated.
  • Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) is caused due to risk of blood clotting, which will then require an effective blood clot treatment for complete recovery.

Skeletal Traction Recovery Plan

A proper skeletal traction recovery plan is significant to ensure a speedy healing process. Whether traction is used for surgery or it is used as an initial step of a treatment, such as closed reduction, a proper, effective recovery plan is essential for healing. To have a safe return to mobility after complex traction such as akin osteotomy, it is essential to follow a clear skeletal traction recovery plan to avoid complications.
  • Careful hospital-based care
  • Anti-inflammatory drugs for pain management
  • Skilled skeletal traction nursing care for monitoring
  • Physical therapy for faster recovery
  • Follow-up appointments and clinical evaluation

Skeletal Traction Recovery Stages: Healing Roadmap

Time Period Focus Area Key Activities
1-2 weeks Immobilization, body stability, and infection control. Have effective nursing care to monitor pin sites.
3-4 weeks Monitoring the healing process Adjust weight and evaluate through laboratory testing.
5-6 weeks Transition to mobilization Start physical therapy, remove traction, and observe bone growth.
7 and ongoing week Complete home recovery Use of a bone stimulator is required, continue physiotherapy.

How Bone Stimulators Support Skeletal Traction Recovery

During the skeletal traction procedure, weights and pulleys are used to correct bone alignment. At times, during this phase, due to age and the complexity of the fracture, the healing process might take time. This is when a bone stimulator helps the patients recover.

When is a Bone Stimulator Useful?

  • The healing process takes time after the surgery.
  • The patient has a previous history of smoking, diabetes, or osteoporosis.
  • The affected area is in weight-bearing bone, such as the femur and tibia.

The Final Thought on Skeletal Traction: Healing with Confidence

In the end, it can be demonstrated that understanding the procedure and complications of skeletal infection not only educates you about this treatment but also helps you take necessary steps during the healing and surgery process. Skeletal traction is used for complex fractures distal femur or proximal tibia and also in broader orthopedic approaches including akin osteotomy, and closed reduction. Are you experiencing symptoms of a skeletal infection or need emergency evaluation? Visit our experienced emergency physicians at the ER of Irving for immediate assessment, diagnostic testing, and coordination with orthopedic specialists for treatment planning and recovery options.

Call Now Get Direction

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

What is skeletal traction?

Skeletal traction is a medical surgery procedure to stabilize a fracture by inserting pins and wires to attach them to weights and pulleys.

What are the complications of skeletal traction?

The most common complications are muscle wasting, pin infection, blood clotting at times, and prolonged instability. With a proper sprains and fracture treatment this condition can be avoided.

Why and why not skeletal traction?

Skeletal traction is preferred in complex fractures, such as for the femur, where splinting is difficult. This surgery is not suitable where the splint or brace cannot be placed or where the skin starts breaking where the pins are inserted.

How long does it take to apply skeletal traction?

The skeletal traction usually takes around 6-8 weeks but can be often increased to 10 weeks for complete recovery.

How to calculate the weight for skeletal infection?

It usually takes around 7kg but differs depending on the severity and body weight. In general, it takes 10% of the body weight.

How to Tell If a Bone Is Fractured or Bruised: Key Signs

Bone injuries, like fractures or bruises, can cause significant pain and confusion. If you’ve taken a fall, been in a sports accident, or experienced trauma, you might wonder, “Is my bone fractured or just bruised?” Knowing the difference is crucial for getting the right care. At ER of Irving, a 24/7 emergency room in Irving, TX, we use Diagnostic Imaging Services to evaluate bone pain and rule out serious injuries. This guide covers the key signs of a fractured or bruised bone, including stress fractures and bruised sternum symptoms, to help you decide when to seek medical attention.

Understanding Bone Injuries: Fractures and Bruises

In some cases, what feels like a bone injury might be related to soft tissue or cartilage issues, such as Slipping Rib Syndrome. This condition often mimics rib fractures or sternum bruises, causing sharp chest or upper abdominal pain. Bone injuries can be confusing because their symptoms overlap. Here’s a detailed breakdown of each:

What Is a Bone Fracture?

A bone fracture occurs when a bone breaks or cracks due to force, stress, or underlying conditions. Fractures range from minor to severe, affecting bones like the femur, wrist, or foot. Common types include:
  • Stress fracture: Hairline cracks from repetitive stress, like running long distances, often start as a dull ache that worsens to sharp pain with activity.
  • Simple fracture: A clean break where bone ends stay aligned, common in falls.
  • Compound fracture: A severe break where the bone pierces the skin, risking infection.
  • Greenstick fracture: A partial break where the bone bends, typical in children due to flexible bones.
  • Comminuted fracture: The bone shatters into multiple pieces, often from high-impact trauma.
Fractures cause intense pain and may alter the bone’s shape, making movement difficult. For example, a fractured foot might prevent walking.

What Is a Bone Bruise?

A bone bruise, or contusion, results from trauma that causes bleeding under the bone’s surface without breaking it. These micro-fractures are less severe but can mimic fractures. Types include:
  • Subperiosteal hematoma: Bleeding under the bone’s outer layer, often in the shins.
  • Interosseous bruise: Damage to the bone marrow, common in the knees or feet.
  • Subchondral bruise: Bleeding between cartilage and bone, seen in joints.
Bone bruises occur in sports collisions, minor falls, or car accidents.

Bone Bruise on the Shin

The shin is one of the most common places for a bone bruise. The shinbone sits just under the skin with little muscle or fat to cushion it. A knock against a table, a step, or a ball can bruise the bone itself. A shin bone bruise usually shows as a tender, swollen spot that aches when you walk or press on it. The skin over it may turn blue or purple. Rest the leg, ice it in short sessions with a cloth between ice and skin, and keep it raised. Get an X-ray if you cannot put weight on the leg, or if the pain gets worse instead of better after a few days.

Symptoms: How to Tell the Difference

How to tell if a bone is broken or just bruised? Or how to tell if a bone is fractured or sprained? Symptoms vary by injury, and understanding them is key. Below is a detailed comparison, including foot-specific injuries : Table: Fracture vs. Bruised Bone vs. Sprain Symptoms
Symptom Fracture Bone Bruise
Pain Sharp, searing, immediate, worsens with movement or weight-bearing Deep, throbbing ache; intensifies with pressure
Swelling Rapid, severe, around the bone Gradual, moderate, diffuse
Deformity Visible None
Mobility Severely limited or impossible Reduced, with stiffness
Sound/Sensation Snap, crack, or grinding at the injury Tenderness, no distinct sound
Bruising May occur, less prominent Prominent, blue-black discoloration

Detailed Symptom Breakdown

Bone Bruise Symptoms:

If you're wondering what a bruised bone feels like, it's typically a deep, internal ache that intensifies with pressure or movement. Common symptoms include swelling, warmth, and visible discoloration like blue or purple hues.

Fracture Symptoms:

Fracture pain is intense and sharp, especially with movement, and doesn’t ease at rest. Swelling and bruising occur around the bone, and the affected area may appear deformed or misaligned. The bone may be immobile, making it difficult or impossible to move or bear weight, like a fractured leg that prevents walking. Tip: If pain radiates to the back, it could resemble back pain, signaling a need for medical evaluation.

What Causes Bone Injuries?

Each injury has distinct causes, often tied to trauma or stress:

Fractures:

Fractures can result from high-impact trauma like falls, car accidents, or workplace injuries. In athletes, repetitive stress from activities like running or dancing may cause stress fractures over time. Weakened bones due to osteoporosis in older adults or growth-related conditions in children also increase the risk of fractures.

Bone Bruises:

Bone bruises commonly occur due to direct impacts or trauma. In sports, collisions or blunt force, like a kick to the shin or a fall, can bruise bones. A typical example is a bruised sternum from seatbelt pressure during a car accident. Foot bones may also bruise from stepping awkwardly on uneven surfaces or dropping heavy objects.

Who Is at Risk for Bone Injuries?

Certain groups are more prone to bone injuries due to age, activity, or health. Athletes face high risks from impact or overuse, often leading to fractures or sprains. Children, with softer bones, are vulnerable to breaks and bruises from falls during play. Older adults are more likely to suffer fractures from minor accidents due to osteoporosis. Manual workers risk injuries like foot fractures from dropped equipment. Those with joint conditions or past sprains are more susceptible to recurring sprains.

How Are Bone Injuries Diagnosed?

Accurate diagnosis is critical to distinguish fractures, bruises, and sprains. Healthcare providers use:

Physical Exam

  • Assessing pain, swelling, and deformity. For a bruised sternum, providers check breathing patterns to rule out cardiac & chest pain.
  • Testing mobility: Fractures limit movement; sprains cause joint looseness.
  • Palpation: Pressing the foot can reveal bruise tenderness vs. fracture pain.

Imaging

  • X-rays: The gold standard for fractures, showing breaks or cracks within seconds. Essential for how to tell whether a bone is fractured or sprained.
  • CT Scans: Detailed views for complex fractures or stress fractures.

Treatment Options and Recovery

Treatment varies by injury, focusing on stabilization and pain relief:

Fracture Treatment:

  • Stabilization: Splints, braces, or casts immobilize the bone. For foot fracture treatment, a boot may be used, while severe fractures sometimes need skeletal traction to align the bone.
  • Pain management: Medications reduce discomfort and are administered carefully.
  • Specialist referral: Orthopedists handle casting or surgery.
  • Recovery: 6–12 weeks, depending on severity. Stress fractures may heal faster with rest.

Bone injuries, like fractures or bruises, can cause significant pain and confusion. If you’ve taken a fall, been in a sports accident, or experienced trauma, you might wonder, “Is my bone fractured or just bruised?” Knowing the difference is crucial for getting the right care.

At ER of Irving, a 24/7 emergency room in Irving, TX, we use Diagnostic Imaging Services to evaluate bone pain and rule out serious injuries. This guide covers the key signs of a fractured or bruised bone, including stress fractures and bruised sternum symptoms, to help you decide when to seek medical attention.

Understanding Bone Injuries: Fractures and Bruises

In some cases, what feels like a bone injury might be related to soft tissue or cartilage issues, such as Slipping Rib Syndrome. This condition often mimics rib fractures or sternum bruises, causing sharp chest or upper abdominal pain. Bone injuries can be confusing because their symptoms overlap. Here’s a detailed breakdown of each:

What Is a Bone Fracture?

A bone fracture occurs when a bone breaks or cracks due to force, stress, or underlying conditions. Fractures range from minor to severe, affecting bones like the femur, wrist, or foot. Common types include:

  • Stress fracture: Hairline cracks from repetitive stress, like running long distances, often start as a dull ache that worsens to sharp pain with activity.
  • Simple fracture: A clean break where bone ends stay aligned, common in falls.
  • Compound fracture: A severe break where the bone pierces the skin, risking infection.
  • Greenstick fracture: A partial break where the bone bends, typical in children due to flexible bones.
  • Comminuted fracture: The bone shatters into multiple pieces, often from high-impact trauma.

Fractures cause intense pain and may alter the bone’s shape, making movement difficult. For example, a fractured foot might prevent walking.

What Is a Bone Bruise?

A bone bruise, or contusion, results from trauma that causes bleeding under the bone’s surface without breaking it. These micro-fractures are less severe but can mimic fractures. Types include:

  • Subperiosteal hematoma: Bleeding under the bone’s outer layer, often in the shins.
  • Interosseous bruise: Damage to the bone marrow, common in the knees or feet.
  • Subchondral bruise: Bleeding between cartilage and bone, seen in joints.

Bone bruises occur in sports collisions, minor falls, or car accidents.

Bone Bruise on the Shin

The shin is one of the most common places for a bone bruise. The shinbone sits just under the skin with little muscle or fat to cushion it. A knock against a table, a step, or a ball can bruise the bone itself.

A shin bone bruise usually shows as a tender, swollen spot that aches when you walk or press on it. The skin over it may turn blue or purple.

Rest the leg, ice it in short sessions with a cloth between ice and skin, and keep it raised. Get an X-ray if you cannot put weight on the leg, or if the pain gets worse instead of better after a few days.

Symptoms: How to Tell the Difference

Swelling Rapid, severe, around the bone Gradual, moderate, diffuse
Deformity Visible None

If you’re wondering what a bruised bone feels like, it’s typically a deep, internal ache that intensifies with pressure or movement. Common symptoms include swelling, warmth, and visible discoloration like blue or purple hues.

Fracture Symptoms:

Fracture pain is intense and sharp, especially with movement, and doesn’t ease at rest. Swelling and bruising occur around the bone, and the affected area may appear deformed or misaligned. The bone may be immobile, making it difficult or impossible to move or bear weight, like a fractured leg that prevents walking.

Fractures:

content.raw:
Slipping Rib Syndrome: Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment

Slipping rib syndrome (SRS), sometimes called clicking rib syndrome, rib-tip syndrome, or interchondral subluxation, is a painful condition caused by the movement of the lower ribs (typically the 8th, 9th, and 10th) due to loosened cartilage attachments. This slipping can compress or irritate surrounding nerves and muscles, leading to pain that can mimic abdominal issues, heart problems, or musculoskeletal disorders. Often underdiagnosed, SRS accounts for a small percentage of chest wall pain cases but can significantly impact quality of life. This comprehensive guide explores the symptoms, causes, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention strategies for slipping rib syndrome, empowering you with the knowledge to seek the right care at the right time.

What Is Slipping Rib Syndrome?

Slipping rib syndrome occurs when the cartilage that holds the lower ribs (false ribs) in place becomes weakened or detached. Unlike true ribs (1st to 7th), which attach directly to the sternum, the false ribs are connected by soft cartilage, making them more prone to hypermobility or dislocation. When these ribs move abnormally, they can rub against or compress nearby intercostal nerves, resulting in pain or a clicking sensation. Also Known As:
  • Clicking rib syndrome
  • Rib-tip syndrome
  • Interchondral subluxation
  • Dislocated or displaced ribs
Our Diagnostic Services at ER of Irving, including X-rays and CT scans, can help identify the cause of such pain.

What Are the Symptoms of Slipping Rib Syndrome?

The symptoms of slipping rib syndrome can be varied, often making it hard to diagnose without a thorough evaluation. Common symptoms include:
  • Sharp or stabbing pain in the lower chest, side, or upper abdomen, worsening with movement.
  • Clicking or popping sensation when moving, breathing, or pressing the rib.
  • Dull ache that lingers after sharp pain episodes.
  • Pain radiating to the back or shoulder, mimicking back pain.
  • Tenderness when touching the affected rib.
Pain may worsen with actions like coughing, twisting, or reaching overhead. In severe cases, SRS can cause breathing problems, making it hard to take deep breaths. If you’re experiencing these, the ER of Irving’s Cardiac & Chest Pain team can rule out serious conditions.

What is the location of the Slipping Rib Syndrome Pain?

Pain is most commonly localized to the lower front rib cage but can radiate to the side, back, or shoulder area, depending on which nerves are affected.

Which Ribs Are Affected by Slipped Rib Syndrome?

Slipping rib syndrome typically affects the 8th, 9th, or 10th ribs, known as false ribs, located at the lower rib cage. Unlike true ribs (1st–7th), false ribs don’t connect directly to the sternum, relying on fibrous ligaments that can weaken, causing hypermobility. This makes them prone to slipping, especially after trauma. Slipping Rib Syndrome at a Glance
Aspect Details
Affected Ribs 8th, 9th, 10th (false ribs)
Pain Location Lower chest, upper abdomen, side, or back
Common Triggers Twisting, coughing, reaching overhead
Diagnostic Tools Hooking maneuver, X-rays, CT scans, ultrasound (ER of Irving)

What Causes Slipping Rib Syndrome?

Several factors can contribute to the onset of slipping rib syndrome, including:
  • Trauma or injury: Falls, sports impacts, or car accidents can loosen rib cartilage, which is common in trauma & injury
  • Repetitive motions: Coughing, lifting, or twisting can strain ligaments.
  • Congenital weakness: Some people have naturally loose rib cartilage.
  • Posture issues: Slouching or scoliosis may misalign ribs over time.
For example, an athlete with a workplace accident or a child with a fall may develop SRS. Our Pediatric Emergencies team can assess younger patients.

Who Is at Risk for Slipping Rib Syndrome?

Certain groups are more likely to develop SRS, including:
  • Athletes: Contact sports (e.g., football, wrestling) increase risk due to impacts.
  • Post-injury patients: Those recovering from chest or abdominal trauma.
  • Children and teens: Growing bodies may have flexible cartilage, seen in pediatric emergencies.
  • People with hypermobility: Conditions like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome weaken ligaments.

How Is Slipping Rib Syndrome Diagnosed?

Proper diagnosis of SRS often involves a combination of physical examination and imaging studies. A common diagnostic technique includes:
  • The Hooking Maneuver: A clinician hooks their fingers under the rib cage and pulls outward to reproduce pain or a popping sensation. This is a widely accepted slipping rib syndrome test.
  • Imaging: While X-rays often do not show cartilage issues, they help rule out fractures. Ultrasound or dynamic imaging may reveal rib movement. CT scans or MRIs may be used to assess for soft tissue damage or rule out other conditions.
It’s essential to differentiate SRS from similar conditions such as:
  • Costochondritis
  • Muscle strain
  • Gallbladder disease
  • Cardiac conditions
  • Pneumonia
Our Laboratory Testing can further assist in ruling out infections or other causes of severe illness.

Treatment Options for Slipping Rib Syndrome?

The treatment plan for slipping rib syndrome depends on the severity and frequency of symptoms. Most cases are managed with conservative care:
  • Pain Management: Over-the-counter pain relievers or prescribed medications to reduce inflammation, administered at the ER of Irving via IV Fluids & Medications for immediate relief.
  • Physical Therapy: Targeted exercises to strengthen core muscles and stabilize the rib cage.
  • Manual Therapy: Mobilization techniques are performed by trained physiotherapists.
  • Activity Modification: Avoiding movements that trigger symptoms, including lifting, twisting, or intense sports.
  • Bracing: In some cases, supportive braces or wraps may help restrict movement.

How do you fix a slipping rib syndrome?

Treatment begins with conservative approaches like rest, posture correction, and physical therapy. If these do not help, intercostal nerve blocks or surgery may be recommended.

What exercises help slipping rib syndrome?

Gentle core-strengthening and posture-corrective exercises can help. These may include:
  • Diaphragmatic breathing
  • Isometric abdominal contractions
  • Gentle spinal extensions
  • Pilates-based core routines
Always consult a physical therapist before starting any slipping rib syndrome exercises to avoid further irritation. If symptoms persist for months and significantly impact daily life, a referral to a specialist such as an orthopedic or thoracic surgeon may be necessary for further intervention.

Can You Prevent Slipping Rib Syndrome?

While not always preventable, you can reduce SRS risk by:
  • Maintaining good posture: Avoid slouching to keep ribs aligned.
  • Strengthening core muscles: Physical therapy can stabilize the rib cage.
  • Avoiding repetitive strain: Limit excessive twisting or lifting.
  • Protecting against trauma: Use proper gear in sports or hazardous work.

When Should You Seek Medical Attention?

Not all rib pain requires emergency care, but you should seek medical help if:
  • The pain is sudden, severe, or worsening
  • You experience difficulty breathing or chest tightness
  • Pain is accompanied by fever, swelling, or redness
  • The discomfort mimics heart pain or radiates to the arm or jaw
Prompt evaluation helps rule out life-threatening conditions and ensures timely relief. If you're experiencing chest or rib pain that’s sharp, persistent, or difficult to explain, don’t wait. The ER of Irving is open 24/7 for chest and rib pain evaluation. Seek emergency care for sudden or severe pain, trouble breathing, fever, or pain that spreads to the arm or jaw.

Call Now Get Direction

Frequently Asked Questions

Can slipping rib syndrome go away on its own?

Yes, mild cases may resolve in weeks with rest, but persistent pain requires ER evaluation.

How long does slipping rib syndrome last?

Pain often subsides in a few weeks, but chronic cases may last months without treatment.

Can slipping rib syndrome cause back pain?

Yes, pain can radiate to the back, mimicking back pain conditions.

Is slipping rib syndrome dangerous?

It’s rarely life-threatening but can cause breathing problems or mimic serious issues, warranting ER care.

What can be mistaken for slipping rib syndrome?

Conditions such as gallbladder attacks, costochondritis, intercostal neuralgia, and even heart disease can mimic SRS symptoms, which is why accurate diagnosis is key.

What triggers slipping rib syndrome pain?

Twisting, coughing, or reaching overhead can worsen pain.

IV for Dehydration: Complete Guide

Dehydration can hit hard and fast, whether it’s from relentless vomiting, a scorching Texas heatwave, or a severe illness like pneumonia. At the ER of Irving, an emergency room in Irving, TX, we see patients daily asking, “What is IV hydration?” and “When do I need an IV for dehydration?” This guide has the answers. From spotting the signs to understanding IV fluids for dehydration in adults and kids, we’ll show you how our ER delivers rapid, life-saving hydration when you need it most. Whether it’s a child with a high fever or an adult with food poisoning, our IV Fluids & Medications team is ready to act.

What Is IV Hydration?

IV hydration is a medical treatment that delivers fluids and electrolytes straight into your bloodstream through an intravenous (IV) line. Unlike drinking water, which takes time to absorb, IVs offer instant rehydration, crucial when dehydration turns dangerous. At the ER of Irving, we use IV hydration to treat emergencies like food poisoning, severe illness, and even stroke & neurological symptoms, where fluids stabilize patients fast.

When Do I Need an IV for Dehydration?

Dehydration isn’t just thirst; it can be an emergency. You might need an IV if you experience:
  • Severe thirst or dry mouth that won’t quit.
  • Dizziness, fainting, or a racing pulse.
  • Dark urine, sunken eyes, or confusion.
Our ER sees this in cases like abdominal pain from appendicitis, severe illnesses like flu complications, or pediatric emergencies with high fevers. If you can’t keep fluids down due to vomiting or diarrhea, an IV becomes critical.

How to Tell If You Need an IV for Dehydration

Not sure if it’s serious? Here’s how to spot it: Pinch your skin if it stays “tented” (slow to bounce back), you’re dehydrated. Extreme weakness, inability to drink, or fainting are red flags too. At the ER of Irving, our Diagnostic Services offer on-site X-rays and lab testing, check your vitals and electrolyte levels fast. Dehydration can also cause back pain or breathing problems, and we’re equipped to diagnose and treat them instantly.

What IV Is Given for Dehydration? The 4 Main Types

When you arrive at the ER of Irving needing an IV for dehydration, we choose from four main IV fluids based on your condition:
  1. Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl) – The best IV fluid for dehydration in most cases, it’s a simple salt-water mix to restore volume.
  2. Lactated Ringer’s – Packed with electrolytes, it’s ideal for trauma & injuries or cardiac & chest pain.
  3. Dextrose 5% in Water (D5W) – Adds sugar for an energy boost, often used after prolonged dehydration.
  4. Half Normal Saline (0.45% NaCl) – Lower salt for milder cases or specific needs.
Here’s a quick comparison:
Fluid Type Best For Notes
Normal Saline General dehydration Saltwater mix
Lactated Ringer’s Severe illness/trauma Electrolyte-rich
Dextrose 5% Energy boost Sugar-based
Half Normal Saline Mild cases Lower salt

How Long Does IV Hydration Last?

An IV session at the ER of Irving takes 30–60 minutes, depending on how dehydrated you are. The effects of better energy and stable vitals can last 1–2 days, though severe cases like blood clot treatment may need ongoing care. Our IV Fluids & Medications team monitors you to ensure full recovery.

IV Fluids for Dehydration: How Many Bags?

How many bags of IV fluid for dehydration? It depends:
  • Mild dehydration: 1 bag (500–1,000 mL) often does the trick.
  • Severe dehydration: 2–3 bags may be needed, especially for appendicitis treatment or gastrointestinal care issues like vomiting.
Note: Only licensed healthcare providers can determine the appropriate treatment plan and dosage of IV fluids. Always consult a medical professional for proper diagnosis and care.

Common Conditions That Cause Dehydration

Common conditions that cause dehydration include:
  • Food poisoning

Can ER Do X-Rays? Everything You Need to Know

When you’re dealing with a sudden injury or illness, waiting hours at an emergency room (ER) for answers isn’t ideal. That’s where ER comes in,  and a common question we hear at the ER of Irving is, "Can ER do X-rays?" The answer is yes, and in this guide, we’ll break down everything you need to know about X-ray services at Emergency rooms, including whether they have the equipment, what conditions they can diagnose, and why they’re a smart choice for fast imaging in Irving, TX.

Do ERs Do X-Rays? The Short Answer

Yes, ER can do X-rays! Most ER facilities, including the ER of Irving, are equipped to perform X-ray imaging to quickly diagnose injuries and illnesses. Over 80% of emergency rooms in the U.S. offer this service, according to industry surveys. Whether you’ve twisted an ankle or suspect a chest infection, emergency rooms are designed to handle these diagnostic needs efficiently.

Do Emergency Rooms Have X-Rays On-Site?

Another question patients often ask is, "Do ERs have X-rays on-site?" In most cases, yes, ER facilities like the ER of Irving have X-ray machines right in-house. This means you don’t have to wait for a referral or travel to a separate imaging center. Having X-rays on-site allows the emergency room to deliver results fast, often within 20–30 minutes, so you can get treatment without delay. Unlike some primary care offices that might send you elsewhere for imaging, ERs’ diagnostic tools are ready when you need them.

Does ER Have X-Ray Services for All Conditions?

You might also wonder, "Does ER have X-ray services for every situation?" ER X-rays are perfect for common conditions like:
  • Fractures or broken bones (e.g., wrist, ankle, or finger injuries)
  • Chest pain issues (e.g., pneumonia or bronchitis)
  • Joint problems (e.g., dislocations or sprains)
At the ER of Irving, our X-ray services are tailored to urgent, non-life-threatening cases. However, for complex issues like internal organ damage or severe trauma, a hospital’s advanced imaging (e.g., CT scans or MRIs) might be required. For most everyday injuries, though, ER has you covered.

What Can Emergency Room X-Rays Detect?

Wondering what emergency room  X-rays can detect? These imaging tools are highly effective for diagnosing:
  • Bone fractures and dislocations
  • Chest Infection and Lung Problems
  • Digestive Issues
  • Urinary tract complications
At the ER of Irving, we combine imaging with fast-track treatment options to give patients a seamless experience from diagnosis to recovery. If your condition is more critical, our emergency room services are ready to handle any urgent medical situation.

What to Expect When Getting an X-Ray at the Emergency Room

If you’re new to ER imaging, here’s what happens when you visit for an X-ray:
  1. Check-In: Walk in (no appointment needed at the ER of Irving) and explain your symptoms.
  2. Imaging: A technician positions you for a quick, painless X-ray, usually taking 5–10 minutes.
  3. Results: A provider reviews the images and discusses findings, often within 20–30 minutes.
X-rays use low levels of radiation, making them safe for most patients. Plus, with on-site equipment, there’s no waiting for lab transfers, perfect for busy schedules in Irving, TX.

When to Choose the Emergency Room for an X-Ray

You should visit ER for an X-ray if you experience:
  • Acute but non-life-threatening pain
  • A sports injury
  • Breathing problems
  • Chest pain
  • Persistent abdominal pain
However, if your symptoms are severe or life-threatening, such as signs of a heart attack or major trauma, please go directly to the emergency room.

Visit the ER of Irving for Fast X-ray services in Irving, TX

Yes, ER can do X-rays, and they are a convenient, cost-effective, and fast option for residents of Irving, TX. From diagnosing fractures to uncovering hidden illnesses, ERs like the ER of Irving are fully equipped to provide high-quality diagnostic services without the hassle of a hospital visit. If you or a loved one needs an X-ray today, don’t wait, visit the ER of Irving or call (972)893-3148 and an on-site X-ray can usually return results within 20 to 30 minutes. Call Now Get Direction

title.rendered: Emergency Room of Irving, TX vs. Urgent Care: What’s the Difference?

content.raw:
Quick answer: If your symptoms could be life threatening, go to the emergency room or call 911. Chest pain, stroke signs, trouble breathing, and heavy bleeding all need emergency care.

Urgent care handles minor illness and injury, but only while it is open. ER of Irving is open 24 hours a day, every day of the year.

This guide explains which conditions belong in each setting, what changes after hours, and how to decide when you are not sure.

When should you go to the emergency room?

Go to the ER for any symptom that could threaten your life, your limb, or your sight. MedlinePlus advises calling 911 when you think a problem is life threatening, even if you are not certain.

Take these symptoms to an emergency room right away:

  • Chest pain or pressure, especially with sweating, nausea, or arm and jaw pain
  • Stroke signs such as face drooping, arm weakness, or slurred speech
  • Trouble breathing or severe shortness of breath
  • Bleeding that will not stop with steady pressure
  • Head injury with confusion, vomiting, or loss of consciousness
  • Seizures, fainting, or a sudden severe headache
  • Severe abdominal pain
  • Suspected poisoning or overdose
  • High fever in a newborn, or a child who will not wake fully

Chest discomfort is the most common heart attack sign, and it usually lasts more than a few minutes. It can feel like pressure, squeezing, or fullness rather than sharp pain, according to MedlinePlus. Women more often report nausea, cold sweats, or unusual fatigue.

When is urgent care the right choice?

Urgent care suits minor problems that still need same day attention. Common examples include mild flu symptoms, small cuts, earaches, and simple urinary infections.

Two things decide it for you. The first is how severe the symptom is. The second is whether urgent care is actually open.

ER or urgent care, condition by condition

Most people search for one symptom, not a general rule. Find yours below. The right column lists the warning signs that move a problem from urgent care to the emergency room.

These red flags follow the MedlinePlus guide on when to use the emergency room. When in doubt, choose the ER.

Condition Usually the right place Go to the ER if
Chest pain Emergency room Always. Chest pain or pressure needs testing to rule out the heart.
Abdominal pain Depends on severity The pain is severe or sudden, sits in the lower right side, or comes with fever or vomiting
Kidney stones Emergency room for severe pain The pain is severe, you have fever or chills, or you cannot keep fluids down
Broken bones Urgent care for a minor break, such as a toe Bone pushes through the skin, the limb looks bent, or you cannot move it or bear weight
Stitches and deep cuts Urgent care for small cuts The wound is deep or gaping, or bleeding will not stop with steady pressure
Vomiting and diarrhea Urgent care It will not stop, you see blood, or you show signs of dehydration
Fever in adults Urgent care Fever comes with a headache and stiff neck, confusion, or trouble breathing, or medicine does not bring it down
Fever in children Depends on age A baby younger than 3 months has any fever, or a child is hard to wake or breathing fast
Head injury Emergency room if symptoms follow The person passed out, is confused, keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache
Urinary tract infection Urgent care You have fever, back or side pain, or vomiting, which can mean a kidney infection
Allergic reaction Urgent care for a mild rash or itching Lips, tongue, or throat swell, or breathing becomes hard. See our anaphylaxis care.
Asthma flare Urgent care for a mild flare Your rescue inhaler does not help, lips look blue, or you cannot finish a sentence
Dizziness Depends on the cause It does not go away, or comes with fainting, chest pain, or weakness on one side
Back pain Urgent care It follows a fall or crash, or comes with leg numbness or loss of bladder control
Burns Urgent care for small, minor burns The burn is large or deep, sits on the face, hands, or groin, or came from electricity or chemicals
Animal bites Urgent care The bite is deep, will not stop bleeding, shows signs of infection, or came from a wild animal
Eye injury Urgent care for minor irritation A chemical splashed in the eye, an object is stuck in it, or your vision suddenly changes
High blood pressure Your doctor, for a high reading with no symptoms A high reading comes with chest pain, a severe headache, vision changes, or confusion
Dehydration Urgent care for mild cases You feel confused or faint, stop urinating, or cannot keep any fluids down
Sore throat Urgent care You have trouble swallowing or breathing, are drooling, or cannot open your mouth fully

If your symptom is not listed, use the same test. Ask whether it could threaten life, limb, or sight. If the answer might be yes, go to the emergency room.

What if it is late at night or on a weekend?

Most urgent care centers around Irving close in the evening and keep shorter weekend hours. An emergency room does not close.

That matters because symptoms rarely wait for business hours. ER of Irving is staffed around the clock by emergency physicians, with lab and imaging on site. If you need care at 2 in the morning in Irving, an emergency room is the option that is open.

ER or urgent care in Irving: a side by side look

Feature Emergency room Urgent care
Best for Life, limb, or sight threatening symptoms Minor illness and injury
Hours Open 24 hours, every day Extended hours, not overnight
Staffing Emergency physicians on site at all times Varies by location and shift
On site testing Advanced imaging and full lab Basic X-ray and lab
Appointment Never needed Walk in or booked
Typical cost Higher, varies by plan Lower, varies by plan

How much does the ER cost compared with urgent care?

An emergency visit generally costs more than an urgent care visit for the same minor problem. MedlinePlus notes that emergency treatment can cost 2 to 3 times more than the same care in your own doctor's office.

The gap comes from what an ER keeps ready. Emergency facilities keep physicians, imaging, and lab staff available at every hour of the day. Many insurance plans also set a higher copay for emergency visits.

Your own cost depends on three things:

  • Your insurance plan and whether you have met your deductible
  • The tests and treatment you need, such as a CT scan or IV fluids
  • Whether your problem turns out to need emergency level care

Federal law also protects you. Under the No Surprises Act, emergency care is billed at your in-network cost sharing, even at an out-of-network facility.

Check your coverage before you need it. Our insurance and billing page lists the plans we work with and explains how to ask about your out of pocket cost.

Never delay care for a life threatening symptom because of cost. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

What about wait times?

Emergency rooms do not see patients in the order they arrive. A nurse checks each patient first, a step called triage. The sickest patients are treated first.

That means a sprained ankle may wait while a possible heart attack goes straight back. Urgent care usually works in arrival order or by booked slot, so the line depends on how many people came before you.

Waits at both change with the day and the hour. Evenings and weekends tend to be busier at urgent care, and many close before the late evening rush. For more on this, see why wait times differ between emergency rooms.

What is a freestanding emergency room?

A freestanding emergency room is a licensed emergency facility that does not sit on a hospital campus. It is open 24 hours, staffed by emergency physicians, and equipped for advanced imaging and lab work.

Freestanding ERs treat the same range of emergencies as any emergency department. When a patient needs surgery, intensive care, or admission, the ER stabilizes them and arranges transfer to a partner hospital.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between urgent care and an emergency room?

Urgent care treats minor illness and injury during set hours. An emergency room treats conditions that could threaten life, limb, or sight, and it stays open 24 hours. Emergency rooms also keep advanced imaging, full lab services, and emergency physicians on site at all times.

Is urgent care cheaper than the emergency room?

Usually, yes, for the same minor problem. Emergency rooms cost more because they keep physicians, imaging, and lab staff ready around the clock. For a true emergency, the ER is the right choice whatever the cost.

Can urgent care do X-rays?

Many urgent care centers have a basic X-ray machine, but most do not offer CT scans or ultrasound. An emergency room has advanced imaging on site at all hours. Read more in our guide on X-rays at the ER.

What happens if urgent care sends me to the ER?

Urgent care staff will send you on if your problem needs tests or treatment they cannot provide. If it is serious, they may call an ambulance. Bring any results or notes they give you so the ER team can start faster.

Can an emergency room treat minor problems too?

Yes. ER of Irving treats fractures, sore throat, rashes, and similar concerns alongside true emergencies. This matters most when urgent care is closed.

Where should I take my child?

Children with a high fever, breathing trouble, dehydration, or a significant injury should be seen in an emergency room. Our pediatric emergency team treats children of all ages, 24 hours a day.

Do I need an appointment?

No. Emergency rooms accept walk in patients at any hour, and no referral is required.

What should I do if I get sick at night and urgent care is closed?

If the problem can safely wait, call your doctor's after hours line or a nurse advice line. If it cannot wait, go to an emergency room. ER of Irving is open all night, every night.

Which is faster, the ER or urgent care?

It depends on how sick you are. Emergency rooms treat the most serious patients first, so a severe problem is seen quickly. For a minor problem, urgent care during open hours is often the shorter wait.

When should I call 911 instead of driving?

Call 911 for chest pain, stroke signs, severe breathing trouble, major trauma, or anyone who is unresponsive. Paramedics begin treatment on the way. MedlinePlus advises calling if you think a problem is life threatening, even when you are unsure.

Call Now Get Directions

If you think you are having a medical emergency, call 911 or go to your nearest emergency room immediately.

Stitches and deep cuts Urgent care for small cuts The wound is deep or gaping, or bleeding will not stop with steady pressure
Vomiting and diarrhea Urgent care It will not stop, you see blood, or you show signs of dehydration
Fever in adults Urgent care Fever comes with a headache and stiff neck, confusion, or trouble breathing, or medicine does not bring it down
Fever in children Depends on age A baby younger than 3 months has any fever, or a child is hard to wake or breathing fast
Head injury Emergency room if symptoms follow The person passed out, is confused, keeps vomiting, or has a worsening headache
Urinary tract infection Urgent care You have fever, back or side pain, or vomiting, which can mean a kidney infection
Allergic reaction Urgent care for a mild rash or itching Lips, tongue, or throat swell, or breathing becomes hard. See our anaphylaxis care.
Asthma flare Urgent care for a mild flare Your rescue inhaler does not help, lips look blue, or you cannot finish a sentence
Dizziness Depends on the cause It does not go away, or comes with fainting, chest pain, or weakness on one side
Back pain Urgent care It follows a fall or crash, or comes with leg numbness or loss of bladder control
Burns Urgent care for small, minor burns The burn is large or deep, sits on the face, hands, or groin, or came from electricity or chemicals
Animal bites Urgent care The bite is deep, will not stop bleeding, shows signs of infection, or came from a wild animal
Eye injury Urgent care for minor irritation A chemical splashed in the eye, an object is stuck in it, or your vision suddenly changes
High blood pressure Your doctor, for a high reading with no symptoms A high reading comes with chest pain, a severe headache, vision changes, or confusion
Dehydration Urgent care for mild cases You feel confused or faint, stop urinating, or cannot keep any fluids down
Sore throat Urgent care You have trouble swallowing or breathing, are drooling, or cannot open your mouth fully

If your symptom is not listed, use the same test. Ask whether it could threaten life, limb, or sight. If the answer might be yes, go to the emergency room.

What if it is late at night or on a weekend?

Most urgent care centers around Irving close in the evening and keep shorter weekend hours. An emergency room does not close.

That matters because symptoms rarely wait for business hours. ER of Irving is staffed around the clock by emergency physicians, with lab and imaging on site. If you need care at 2 in the morning in Irving, an emergency room is the option that is open.

ER or urgent care in Irving: a side by side look

Feature Emergency room Urgent care
Best for Life, limb, or sight threatening symptoms Minor illness and injury
Hours Open 24 hours, every day Extended hours, not overnight
Staffing Emergency physicians on site at all times Varies by location and shift
On site testing Advanced imaging and full lab Basic X-ray and lab
Appointment Never needed Walk in or booked
Typical cost Higher, varies by plan Lower, varies by plan

How much does the ER cost compared with urgent care?

An emergency visit generally costs more than an urgent care visit for the same minor problem. MedlinePlus notes that emergency treatment can cost 2 to 3 times more than the same care in your own doctor’s office.

The gap comes from what an ER keeps ready. Emergency facilities keep physicians, imaging, and lab staff available at every hour of the day. Many insurance plans also set a higher copay for emergency visits.

Your own cost depends on three things:

  • Your insurance plan and whether you have met your deductible
  • The tests and treatment you need, such as a CT scan or IV fluids
  • Whether your problem turns out to need emergency level care

Federal law also protects you. Under the No Surprises Act, emergency care is billed at your in-network cost sharing, even at an out-of-network facility.

Check your coverage before you need it. Our insurance and billing page lists the plans we work with and explains how to ask about your out of pocket cost.

Never delay care for a life threatening symptom because of cost. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

What about wait times?

Emergency rooms do not see patients in the order they arrive. A nurse checks each patient first, a step called triage. The sickest patients are treated first.

That means a sprained ankle may wait while a possible heart attack goes straight back. Urgent care usually works in arrival order or by booked slot, so the line depends on how many people came before you.

Waits at both change with the day and the hour. Evenings and weekends tend to be busier at urgent care, and many close before the late evening rush. For more on this, see why wait times differ between emergency rooms.

What is a freestanding emergency room?

A freestanding emergency room is a licensed emergency facility that does not sit on a hospital campus. It is open 24 hours, staffed by emergency physicians, and equipped for advanced imaging and lab work.

Freestanding ERs treat the same range of emergencies as any emergency department. When a patient needs surgery, intensive care, or admission, the ER stabilizes them and arranges transfer to a partner hospital.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between urgent care and an emergency room?

Urgent care treats minor illness and injury during set hours. An emergency room treats conditions that could threaten life, limb, or sight, and it stays open 24 hours. Emergency rooms also keep advanced imaging, full lab services, and emergency physicians on site at all times.

Is urgent care cheaper than the emergency room?

Usually, yes, for the same minor problem. Emergency rooms cost more because they keep physicians, imaging, and lab staff ready around the clock. For a true emergency, the ER is the right choice whatever the cost.

Can urgent care do X-rays?

Many urgent care centers have a basic X-ray machine, but most do not offer CT scans or ultrasound. An emergency room has advanced imaging on site at all hours. Read more in our guide on X-rays at the ER.

What happens if urgent care sends me to the ER?

Urgent care staff will send you on if your problem needs tests or treatment they cannot provide. If it is serious, they may call an ambulance. Bring any results or notes they give you so the ER team can start faster.

Can an emergency room treat minor problems too?

Yes. ER of Irving treats fractures, sore throat, rashes, and similar concerns alongside true emergencies. This matters most when urgent care is closed.

Where should I take my child?

Children with a high fever, breathing trouble, dehydration, or a significant injury should be seen in an emergency room. Our pediatric emergency team treats children of all ages, 24 hours a day.

Do I need an appointment?

No. Emergency rooms accept walk in patients at any hour, and no referral is required.

What should I do if I get sick at night and urgent care is closed?

If the problem can safely wait, call your doctor’s after hours line or a nurse advice line. If it cannot wait, go to an emergency room. ER of Irving is open all night, every night.

Which is faster, the ER or urgent care?

It depends on how sick you are. Emergency rooms treat the most serious patients first, so a severe problem is seen quickly. For a minor problem, urgent care during open hours is often the shorter wait.

When should I call 911 instead of driving?

Call 911 for chest pain, stroke signs, severe breathing trouble, major trauma, or anyone who is unresponsive. Paramedics begin treatment on the way. MedlinePlus advises calling if you think a problem is life threatening, even when you are unsure.

Call Now Get Directions

If you think you are having a medical emergency, call 911 or go to your nearest emergency room immediately.

This policy explains what cookies are, which ones erofirving.com uses, and how you can control them in your browser.

Effective date: August 26, 2026

What are cookies

Cookies are small text files placed on your computer or mobile device when you visit a website. They help websites work more efficiently, give visitors a better experience, and provide information to the website owner.

How we use cookies

ER of Irving uses cookies for the following purposes:

  • Essential cookies: needed for the website to function, including security, network management, and accessibility.
  • Analytics cookies: Google Analytics helps us understand how visitors use the website so we can improve it.
  • Functionality cookies: remember your preferences and settings.
  • Marketing cookies: may track your online activity to help advertisers show more relevant advertising or limit how many times you see an ad.

Types of cookies we use

  • Session cookies: temporary cookies that expire when you close your browser. They keep your session going as you move through the website.
  • Persistent cookies: stay on your device for a set period or until you delete them. They remember your preferences for future visits.
  • First-party cookies: set directly by ER of Irving to improve functionality and performance.
  • Third-party cookies: set by partners such as Google Analytics to analyze website usage.

Managing your cookie preferences

You can decide whether to accept or reject cookies by:

  • Changing your browser settings to refuse all or some cookies.
  • Deleting cookies that have already been set.
  • Installing the Google Analytics opt-out browser add-on.

If you block or delete cookies, some features of the website may not work properly. Most browsers explain cookie controls in their help section: Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Safari, and Microsoft Edge.

Google Analytics

We use Google Analytics to analyze website traffic and usage patterns. Its cookies collect information in an anonymous form, including the number of visitors, where they come from, and the pages they visit. We use these reports to improve the website.

Healthcare privacy considerations

Cookies on our public website do not collect Protected Health Information (PHI) as defined by HIPAA. Any health information you provide through a secure patient channel is covered by our HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices, not this cookie policy. Our Privacy Policy explains the other information the website collects.

Updates to this cookie policy

We may update this policy to reflect changes in technology, legislation, or our practices. The effective date at the top of this page shows when it was last revised.

title.raw: Billing Disclosures and Patient Financial Rights
title.rendered: Billing Disclosures and Patient Financial Rights

content.raw:
ER of Irving believes in full transparency about your care and its cost. This page carries the state and federal disclosures about our billing practices, insurance networks, and your rights as a patient.

Effective date: August 26, 2026

1. Texas freestanding emergency center disclosures

In compliance with Texas law (Senate Bill 425 and Senate Bill 1151) for freestanding emergency medical care facilities, ER of Irving makes the following disclosures:

  • This facility is a freestanding emergency medical care facility.
  • This facility charges rates comparable to a hospital emergency room and may charge a facility fee.
  • This facility or a physician providing medical care at the facility may be an out-of-network provider for the patient's health benefit plan network.
  • The physician providing medical care at the facility may bill separately from the facility for the medical care provided to a patient.
  • This facility is not a participating provider in any state or federal health care program, including Medicare, Medicaid, and Tricare.

To find out whether our facility is in-network with your plan, contact your insurance provider directly or ask our front desk staff before receiving non-life-threatening treatment.

2. Your rights and protections against surprise medical bills (No Surprises Act)

When you get emergency care, or are treated by an out-of-network provider at an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center, you are protected from surprise billing, also called balance billing.

What is balance billing? When you see a provider, you may owe out-of-pocket costs such as a copayment, coinsurance, or a deductible. You may have other costs, or pay the whole bill, if you visit a provider or facility that is not in your plan's network. Out-of-network providers may bill you for the difference between what your plan agreed to pay and the full amount charged. This is balance billing. The amount is often more than in-network costs for the same service and might not count toward your annual out-of-pocket limit.

You are protected from balance billing for emergency services. If you have an emergency medical condition and get emergency services from an out-of-network provider or facility, the most they may bill you is your plan's in-network cost-sharing amount (such as copayments and coinsurance). You cannot be balance billed for these emergency services. This includes services you may get after you are in stable condition, unless you give written consent and give up your protections for those post-stabilization services.

When balance billing is not allowed, you also have these protections:

  • You are only responsible for your share of the cost (the copayments, coinsurance, and deductibles you would pay if the provider or facility were in-network). Your health plan pays out-of-network providers and facilities directly.
  • Your health plan generally must cover emergency services without prior authorization, cover emergency services by out-of-network providers, base your cost-sharing on what it would pay an in-network provider and show that amount in your explanation of benefits, and count any amount you pay for emergency or out-of-network services toward your deductible and out-of-pocket limit.

If you believe you have been wrongly billed, contact the Texas Department of Insurance at 1-800-252-3439 or www.tdi.texas.gov. You may also call the federal No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059 or visit www.cms.gov/nosurprises.

3. Right to a Good Faith Estimate (uninsured or self-pay patients)

Under federal law, health care providers must give patients who do not have insurance, or who are not using insurance, an estimate of the bill for medical items and services.

  • You have the right to receive a Good Faith Estimate for the total expected cost of any non-emergency items or services, including related costs such as tests, prescription drugs, equipment, and facility fees.
  • Ask for a Good Faith Estimate in writing at least one business day before your service. You can also ask any provider you choose for one before you schedule a service.
  • If you receive a bill that is at least $400 more than your Good Faith Estimate, you can dispute the bill.
  • Keep a copy or a photo of your Good Faith Estimate.

For more information about your right to a Good Faith Estimate, visit www.cms.gov/nosurprises.

If you have questions about your bill, our insurance networks, or our financial policies, contact our billing department:

Phone: (972) 893-3148

ER of Irving respects the privacy of everyone who visits erofirving.com. This policy explains what information the website collects, how we use it, and the choices you have.

Effective date: August 26, 2026

Scope of this policy

This policy applies only to your use of this website and the digital data collected here. It does not cover Protected Health Information (PHI) collected during medical treatment.

For how we handle medical records and PHI, please read our separate HIPAA Notice of Privacy Practices. If you do not agree with this policy, please do not use the website.

1. Information we collect

We may collect information about you in several ways when you interact with the website:

  • Personal data: your name, email address, and telephone number when you fill out a contact form or use another feature that asks for them.
  • Usage data: information our servers record automatically, such as your IP address, browser type, operating system, access times, and the pages you viewed before and after visiting the website.
  • Cookies and tracking technologies: small files and tags that help the website work and let us measure how it is used. See our Cookie Policy for details and how to control them.

2. How we use your information

We use the information collected through the website to:

  • Respond to your questions, requests, and contact form submissions.
  • Improve the website, its content, and our outreach.
  • Monitor and analyze usage and trends so the site works better for visitors.
  • Send administrative information or updates about the facility.
  • Protect the website against malicious activity or fraud.

Please do not submit sensitive medical information through the standard website contact forms. Medical questions should be discussed in person, by phone, or through a secure patient channel.

3. Disclosure of your information

We do not sell, trade, or rent your personal information to third parties. We may share information in these situations:

  • Service providers: companies that perform services for us, such as website hosting, data analysis, email delivery, and customer service.
  • By law or to protect rights: when we believe disclosure is needed to respond to legal process, investigate possible violations of our policies, or protect the rights, property, and safety of others, as permitted or required by law.

4. Third-party websites and analytics

The website may link to third-party websites and applications, including social media platforms. Once you leave the website, any information you provide to those third parties is not covered by this policy, and we cannot guarantee its safety.

We may also use vendors such as Google Analytics, which place first-party and third-party cookies to analyze how visitors use the website, measure the popularity of content, and understand online activity.

5. Data security

We use administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to help protect your personal information. No security measure is perfect, and no method of data transmission can be guaranteed against interception or misuse.

6. Policy for children

We do not knowingly collect information from or market to children under 13. If you become aware of data we have collected from a child under 13, please contact us using the details below.

7. Changes to this policy

We may update this policy to reflect changes in our practices or for operational, legal, or regulatory reasons. When we do, we update the effective date at the top of this page. Please review it from time to time.

title.raw: Accessibility Statement
title.rendered: Accessibility Statement

content.rendered:
Accessibility

Accessibility Statement

ER of Irving wants every patient and family member to be able to read our pages, find our address, and call us without barriers. We are working to make erofirving.com conform to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA.

Call (972) 893-3148
Email info@erofirving.com

What we have done

These measures were applied in August 2026 after a full audit with axe-core in a real browser and manual keyboard checks. We re-test after every change.

Colour contrast

Text, link, and button colours meet the 4.5 to 1 minimum across the site.

Keyboard access

Every link, button, and form field shows a visible focus ring. The skip link lands after the header on every page.

Heading order

Each page has one main heading and a logical heading order, so screen readers announce the structure in sequence.

Text alternatives

Images that carry meaning have alt text. Decorative images are hidden from screen readers.

Named links

Citation links that had no readable name were repaired, and links inside articles are underlined so they do not rely on colour.

Ongoing testing

We audit the site after changes and act on accessibility reports within two business days.

How to report a problem

If a page, document, or feature is hard to use, tell us. Here is what happens next.

1

Tell us what happened

Call (972) 893-3148, answered 24 hours a day, or email info@erofirving.com. Include the web address, a short description of the problem, and the assistive technology you were using.

2

We reply within two business days

A team member confirms the report and gives you the information or help you needed another way, by phone if that is easier.

3

We fix and re-test

Confirmed problems are corrected as quickly as we can, then the page is re-tested with automated tools and a keyboard pass.

Questions about this statement

Which standard does ER of Irving follow?

We follow the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 at Level AA, published by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). These guidelines explain how to make web content usable for people who use screen readers, keyboard navigation, or magnification.

Is the website fully compliant?

No website can promise that. Our pages are partially conformant with WCAG 2.1 Level AA: the main pages pass automated and keyboard testing, and some third-party parts do not. We keep testing and fixing, and this page is updated when the site changes.

What are the known limitations?

The embedded Google map and content shown inside social media embeds are provided by third parties and may not fully meet WCAG 2.1 AA. If you cannot use one of them, call us and we will give you directions or the information by phone.

What are my rights?

Nothing on this page changes your rights under the Americans with Disabilities Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, or Texas law. If we do not resolve your concern, you may contact the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights at hhs.gov/ocr or 1-800-368-1019.

Need help right now?

If you cannot use part of this site, call us and we will help by phone. In a medical emergency, call 911 or come to the ER at any time. We are open 24 hours a day at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX 75063.

Call (972) 893-3148
Get Directions

Your Privacy, Protected

Notice of Privacy Practices

This notice describes how medical information about you may be used and disclosed, and how you can get access to this information. Please review it carefully.

Call (972) 893-3148
Contact Us

Our Commitment to Your Privacy

Federal law (HIPAA) requires us to keep your health information private. It also requires us to give you this notice and to follow what it says.

  • We protect every record we create or receive about your care
  • If a breach ever affects your information, we tell you promptly
  • We share only the minimum information each task needs
  • We never sell your information. Marketing uses need your written permission first

Questions? Call (972) 893-3148 and ask for the privacy officer, or email info@erofirving.com.

Effective date: July 13, 2026

How We May Use and Share Your Health Information

For these routine purposes, the law lets us use your information without separate written permission.

Treatment

Our team shares your information with the hospitals and specialists who continue your care.

Payment

We send information to your health plan to bill your visit and confirm coverage.

Health Care Operations

We use records to improve quality, train staff, and run the facility well.

When Required by Law

We disclose information when federal, state, or local law says we must.

Other Situations Where We May Share Information

In limited cases set by law, we may also share information without your authorization.

Public health and safety

We may report to public health authorities. Examples: disease control, suspected abuse or neglect, and product safety. We may also share information to prevent a serious threat to someone’s health or safety.

Health oversight and government functions

Oversight agencies may see records for audits, investigations, and licensing. The same applies to certain government programs, such as military, national security, and workers’ compensation.

Legal proceedings and law enforcement

We may respond to a court order, a subpoena, or another lawful request. We share with law enforcement only in the specific situations the law permits.

Coroners, organ donation, and research

We may share information with coroners and medical examiners, and with organ procurement organizations. Research projects may use records only after an oversight board approves privacy safeguards.

Uses that always need your written permission

Marketing and any sale of information always require your written authorization. So does most anything else this notice does not describe. You can revoke an authorization at any time in writing.

Your Rights Over Your Health Information

You have these rights under HIPAA. To use any of them, call us or send a written request.

Get a Copy of Your Records

See or receive an electronic or paper copy of your record, usually within 30 days. A reasonable, cost-based fee may apply.

Ask Us to Correct Them

If something looks wrong or incomplete, ask us to amend it. If we decline, we explain why in writing within 60 days.

Get a List of Disclosures

Request an accounting of the times we shared your information, covering up to six years.

Request Restrictions

Ask us to limit what we share. Pay fully out of pocket and we must keep that visit from your health plan if you ask.

Confidential Communications

Ask us to contact you only a certain way, such as one phone number or address. We honor reasonable requests.

A Paper Copy of This Notice

Ask any time, even if you chose electronic delivery. We provide one promptly.

Complaints, Questions, and Changes

If you believe your privacy rights were violated, you can file a complaint. We never retaliate against anyone for filing one.

  • With us: Privacy Officer, ER of Irving, 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX 75063. Call (972) 893-3148 or email info@erofirving.com
  • With the government: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights, at hhs.gov/ocr/complaints or 1-800-368-1019

We can change the terms of this notice. Changes apply to all information we hold about you. The current notice is always on this page and on paper at our front desk.

Call (972) 893-3148 and ask for the privacy officer, or visit us at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX 75063. A paper copy is available at the front desk any time.

content.raw:
Letter of Protection (LOP)

Letter of Protection Care at ER of Irving

Hurt in an accident that was not your fault? If you have a personal injury attorney, ER of Irving can treat you under a Letter of Protection. You get full emergency care now and pay from your settlement later. No upfront cost. Open 24/7 in Irving, near Las Colinas and Valley Ranch.

Call (972) 893-3148 Get Directions

What Is a Letter of Protection?

A Letter of Protection, or LOP, is a written agreement between you, your personal injury attorney, and ER of Irving. Your attorney sends us the letter. It promises that your emergency bill will be paid from the money you recover in your case.

This lets you get care right away, even if you cannot pay at the time of your visit. You focus on healing. Your attorney handles the paperwork. We document everything your case needs.

How the process works

  1. Your attorney drafts the LOP and sends it to our team.
  2. We verify the letter and confirm your legal representation.
  3. You receive full emergency care with no upfront payment.
  4. We prepare detailed records, imaging, and physician notes.
  5. Your bill is paid from the settlement when your case resolves.

Why Injured Patients Choose ER of Irving for LOP Care

Freestanding emergency care built for accident recovery and the documentation your case needs.

Seen Right Away

No appointment needed. Our team begins your evaluation promptly, any hour of the day or night.

Imaging and Labs On-Site

CT, X-ray, ultrasound, and lab work happen in one visit, so your injuries are documented the same day.

Records Built for Your Case

We prepare physician notes, imaging reports, and clinical records with the detail injury claims require.

Open 24/7, Every Day

ER of Irving is open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, including weekends and holidays.

Injury Cases Treated Under an LOP

A Letter of Protection applies when another party's negligence caused your injuries and you have legal representation.

Car and Truck Collisions

Whiplash, fractures, head injuries, and internal trauma from auto and commercial vehicle crashes.

Motorcycle and Rideshare Crashes

High-impact injuries from motorcycle wrecks and rideshare collisions as a driver or passenger.

Pedestrian and Cyclist Injuries

Injuries to pedestrians and cyclists struck by a negligent driver on Irving area roads.

Workplace Accidents

Falls, machinery injuries, and other on-the-job trauma tied to a third-party claim.

Slip and Fall Injuries

Falls at stores, restaurants, and apartment complexes caused by unsafe conditions.

Dog Bites and Assault Injuries

Bite wounds and injuries from an attack where another party is at fault.

Letter of Protection vs. Medical Lien

Both options let you get emergency care before your case resolves. They are not the same. The table below shows how a Letter of Protection compares with a medical lien.

FeatureLetter of ProtectionMedical Lien
Who agrees to itYou, your attorney, and ER of IrvingFiled by a provider against your claim
PrivacyStays private between the partiesCan become part of the public record
When the bill is paidFrom your settlementFrom your settlement
Collections while your case is openNot pursued during the caseMay be pursued during the case

Emergency Services Available Under an LOP

Complete emergency evaluation and treatment, all under one roof.

Diagnostic Imaging

On-site CT, digital X-ray, and ultrasound to find fractures, internal injuries, and soft-tissue damage.

Laboratory Testing

Blood counts, metabolic panels, and toxicology run in our on-site lab for fast results.

Stabilization and Treatment

IV fluids, wound care, pain management, splinting, and continuous monitoring by our team.

Injury Documentation

Physician notes and imaging reports that clearly connect your injuries to the accident.

For Personal Injury Attorneys

ER of Irving works directly with personal injury firms across Irving, Las Colinas, Valley Ranch, Coppell, and the wider DFW area. We make LOP coordination simple for your office and your client.

How to refer a client

  • Have your client walk in any time, or call ahead to coordinate.
  • Send the signed Letter of Protection to our billing team.
  • We treat your client and prepare litigation-ready records.
  • We keep your office informed throughout the process.

To set up LOP coordination, call (972) 893-3148.

Letter of Protection FAQs

Do I need health insurance to be treated under an LOP?

No. A Letter of Protection lets you receive care without insurance and without paying upfront. Your attorney guarantees payment from your settlement.

Can my attorney send the LOP before I arrive?

Yes. Your attorney can send the signed letter to our billing team ahead of time. You can also walk in first and have the letter follow.

What happens if my case does not settle?

The terms depend on the agreement your attorney signs with us. Ask your attorney how your specific Letter of Protection handles an unresolved case.

What should the Letter of Protection include?

It should name you, your attorney, and ER of Irving, and confirm that your bill will be paid from your case proceeds. Your attorney prepares the correct wording.

Does the LOP cover follow-up visits?

An LOP at ER of Irving covers the emergency care you receive here. Follow-up care with other providers is arranged separately through your attorney.

Which areas does ER of Irving serve for LOP patients?

We serve Irving, Las Colinas, Valley Ranch, Coppell, Grand Prairie, Farmers Branch, and the surrounding DFW communities.

Is this page legal advice?

No. This page explains how ER of Irving works with Letters of Protection. For advice about your claim, speak with your personal injury attorney.

Injured in an Accident? Get Emergency Care Now

Walk in 24/7 or call ahead. ER of Irving is at 8200 N MacArthur Blvd, Suite 110, Irving, TX 75063. If your condition is life-threatening, call 911.

Call (972) 893-3148 Get Directions
