title.rendered: Editorial and Medical Review Policy

content.raw:
Editorial and Medical Review Policy

At ER of Irving, people across Irving and the surrounding area count on our website for clear health information, often during stressful moments. Because that information can shape real health decisions, we hold every page to a clear standard for how it is written, reviewed, and kept current. This page explains how we work.

Last updated: June 2026.

Who writes our content

Our articles and service pages are written and maintained by the ER of Irving editorial team. Our writers research each topic using trusted medical sources, then write it in plain language so it is easy to follow when it matters.

How our content is medically reviewed

Before we publish anything that covers a medical topic, a qualified medical professional on our team reviews it for accuracy and clarity.

Reviewed by: Rina Rios, RN, Director at ER of Irving

Our reviewer checks that the content reflects current medical guidance, that symptoms and treatments are described correctly, and that nothing could mislead you about when to seek emergency care.

Our editorial decisions are guided by accuracy and patient safety, never by advertisers or sponsors.

The sources we rely on

We base our health content on respected, authoritative sources, including:

  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
  • National Institutes of Health (NIH) and MedlinePlus
  • American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP)
  • American Heart Association (AHA)
  • Peer-reviewed medical journals and established clinical guidelines

When we state a fact or a statistic, we aim to link it back to the original source so you can read more.

How often we update our content

Medical guidance changes over time. We review our health content regularly and refresh it at least once a year, or sooner when new research or guidance appears. Where possible, a page shows when it was last reviewed or updated.

Corrections and feedback

If something looks inaccurate or out of date, we want to hear about it. Reach out through our contact page and our team will look into it promptly.

A note about medical emergencies

The information on this site is for general education only. It is not a diagnosis, a treatment plan, or a substitute for advice from a medical professional who knows your situation. If you think you are having a medical emergency, call 911 or come straight to ER of Irving. We are open 24 hours a day, every day.

Editorial and Medical Review Policy

At ER of Irving, people across Irving and the surrounding area count on our website for clear health information, often during stressful moments. Because that information can shape real health decisions, we hold every page to a clear standard for how it is written, reviewed, and kept current. This page explains how we work.

Last updated: June 2026.

Who writes our content

Our articles and service pages are written and maintained by the ER of Irving editorial team. Our writers research each topic using trusted medical sources, then write it in plain language so it is easy to follow when it matters.

How our content is medically reviewed

Before we publish anything that covers a medical topic, a qualified medical professional on our team reviews it for accuracy and clarity.

Reviewed by: Rina Rios, RN, Director at ER of Irving

Our reviewer checks that the content reflects current medical guidance, that symptoms and treatments are described correctly, and that nothing could mislead you about when to seek emergency care.

Our editorial decisions are guided by accuracy and patient safety, never by advertisers or sponsors.

The sources we rely on

We base our health content on respected, authoritative sources, including:

  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
  • National Institutes of Health (NIH) and MedlinePlus
  • American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP)
  • American Heart Association (AHA)
  • Peer-reviewed medical journals and established clinical guidelines

When we state a fact or a statistic, we aim to link it back to the original source so you can read more.

How often we update our content

Medical guidance changes over time. We review our health content regularly and refresh it at least once a year, or sooner when new research or guidance appears. Where possible, a page shows when it was last reviewed or updated.

Corrections and feedback

If something looks inaccurate or out of date, we want to hear about it. Reach out through our contact page and our team will look into it promptly.

A note about medical emergencies

The information on this site is for general education only. It is not a diagnosis, a treatment plan, or a substitute for advice from a medical professional who knows your situation. If you think you are having a medical emergency, call 911 or come straight to ER of Irving. We are open 24 hours a day, every day.

TL;DR: Emergency trauma care is the rapid evaluation and stabilization of injuries from car crashes, falls, workplace incidents, or assaults. ER of Irving is a Texas-licensed freestanding emergency medical care facility (FEMCF) open 24/7. We handle the initial trauma workup (imaging, bleeding control, fracture splinting, pain control, neuro exam, IV fluids) and coordinate transfer to a Level I or II trauma center when injuries require operative surgery or ICU admission.

What Is Emergency Trauma Care?

Trauma care is the structured, time-critical response to injury. The first hour after a serious injury is the trauma "golden hour," when rapid evaluation and stabilization most improve survival. The Texas Department of State Health Services classifies trauma facilities by capability (Level I through IV), and freestanding ERs serve as the entry point for initial assessment, imaging, and stabilization in most North Texas neighborhoods.

Common Trauma Mechanisms We See

  • Motor vehicle crashes on Hwy 114, Hwy 183, I-635 LBJ, SH 161, and I-30 corridors. See our Hwy 114/183 car-accident guide for corridor-specific patterns.
  • Falls in older adults (the leading cause of injury-related ER visits in U.S. adults over 65)
  • Workplace injuries including Las Colinas worksite incidents
  • Sports injuries, including high-school football, soccer, and weekend recreational
  • Bicycle and pedestrian crashes
  • Domestic injuries (kitchen, garage, yard)

The Texas Trauma Tier System

Texas designates trauma centers by capability, defined under Texas H&S Code Chapter 254:

LevelCapabilityTypical Setting
IComprehensive 24/7 trauma surgery, research, educationMajor academic medical centers
IIComprehensive trauma surgery, may transfer most complex casesLarge community hospitals
IIIPrompt assessment, resuscitation, surgical intervention, stabilization, transferCommunity hospitals
IVAdvanced trauma life support before transfer to higher-level centerRural and community hospitals, FECs

ER of Irving serves as the initial-evaluation and stabilization point for trauma in our service area. For polytrauma, penetrating injuries to the chest or abdomen, or unstable head injuries, we stabilize and transfer to a Level I or II trauma center such as Parkland or Baylor downtown.

Trauma Warning Signs That Need the ER

Visit ER of Irving (or call 911) for any of the following after an injury:

  • Loss of consciousness, even briefly
  • Persistent vomiting
  • Severe headache that worsens
  • Confusion or behavior change (see Concussion and TBI pillars)
  • Suspected broken bone or visible deformity (see Fractures Treatment)
  • Chest pain or shortness of breath after a crash (potential pneumothorax or cardiac contusion, see Heart Attack page)
  • Abdominal pain after blunt impact (potential internal bleeding)
  • Deep lacerations that will not stop bleeding
  • Numbness or weakness in any limb
  • Severe back or neck pain after impact
  • Visible bone, blood that spurts, or massive blood loss

How ER of Irving Stabilizes Trauma

Our trauma workup follows the standard primary-secondary survey:

  1. Primary survey (ABCDE). Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neurologic), Exposure.
  2. Cervical-spine precautions. Collar in place until imaging clears the spine.
  3. IV access and fluid resuscitation. Two large-bore IVs, normal saline for hemorrhagic shock.
  4. Imaging. CT head, cervical spine, chest, abdomen, pelvis. X-rays for suspected fractures. Bedside ultrasound (FAST exam) for internal bleeding.
  5. Wound care. Bleeding control, deep laceration repair, tetanus update.
  6. Pain control. IV analgesics titrated to severity.
  7. Splinting. Suspected fractures stabilized in plaster or fiberglass.
  8. Hospital coordination. Transfer arranged to Level I or II trauma center if operative surgery, ICU monitoring, or advanced subspecialty care is needed.

Local Trauma Corridors We See Most

Three Irving-area road corridors generate the bulk of our motor-vehicle trauma:

  • Hwy 114 and Hwy 183 (Airport Freeway) through Las Colinas and Irving. High speeds, frequent merges, common rear-end collisions.
  • I-635 LBJ through Farmers Branch and Addison. Stop-and-go traffic, sudden-stop chain crashes.
  • SH 161 / President George Bush Tpke between Grand Prairie and Coppell. High-speed single-vehicle and merge collisions.

If you are involved in a crash on any of these, paramedics can route you directly to our facility for initial evaluation. For background, see our Hwy 114/183 car-accident injury guide.

When to Call 911 vs Drive

Call 911 for:

  • Anyone unconscious after a crash or fall
  • Severe bleeding that does not stop with direct pressure
  • Possible spine or neck injury (do not move the person)
  • Crash with rollover, ejection, or fatality in the same vehicle
  • Pedestrian or cyclist struck by a vehicle
  • Chest pain or shortness of breath after blunt chest trauma

Drive to ER of Irving only for mild-to-moderate injuries where the patient is alert, stable, and can be safely transported by car. When in doubt, call.

After-Trauma Care

Recovery extends past the initial ER visit. Expect:

  • Orthopedic follow-up within 1 week for fractures
  • Concussion-clearance protocol for any head injury (see our Concussion Treatment pillar)
  • Physical therapy referral for soft-tissue and joint injuries
  • DVT prevention awareness for anyone immobilized after surgery or fracture (see our Blood Clot page)
  • Mental health screening, since post-traumatic stress is common after motor-vehicle crashes
  • Documentation for insurance or legal claims, including a copy of the ER record

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a freestanding ER handle a car accident?

Yes. Freestanding emergency medical care facilities in Texas are licensed to provide initial trauma assessment, imaging, bleeding control, fracture stabilization, and resuscitation, then arrange transfer to a higher-level trauma center when operative surgery is needed. For most everyday MVCs, the workup is complete at the FEC.

Will my auto insurance pay for an ER visit after a crash?

Texas auto policies often include MedPay or PIP (Personal Injury Protection) coverage for medical bills regardless of fault. The federal No Surprises Act also protects patients from balance billing for emergency care. ER of Irving accepts most major insurance and posts disclosures per Texas Department of Insurance rules.

Do I need an ER visit if I feel fine after a low-speed crash?

Sometimes. Soft-tissue injuries (whiplash, contusions) can take 24 to 48 hours to declare themselves. Internal bleeding can do the same. A same-day evaluation creates a documented baseline that helps if symptoms develop later. Adrenaline often masks pain in the first few hours.

What about pediatric trauma?

We evaluate pediatric trauma using age-appropriate Broselow tools and equipment, and we transfer to Children's Health Dallas or Cook Children's Fort Worth when subspecialty pediatric trauma surgery is required.

Will my insurance cover this?

ER of Irving is a Texas-licensed freestanding emergency medical care facility. Per the federal No Surprises Act and Texas Department of Insurance balance-billing rules, patients are protected from balance billing for emergency care. We post all required disclosures under Texas H&S Code Chapter 254 and can discuss costs with you on arrival.

Visit ER of Irving for 24/7 Trauma Emergency Care

Trauma is the leading cause of death for Americans under 45. The first hour after injury matters most, and a clean ER evaluation is the foundation of every downstream treatment plan. ER of Irving is open 24/7/365 for initial trauma stabilization and transfer coordination.

For corridor-specific patterns, see our Hwy 114/183 car-accident guide and Las Colinas Workplace Injuries. For fractures, head injuries, or concussions, see our Fractures Treatment, Head Injury, and Concussion service pages. For non-emergency questions, use our Contact Us form. When seconds matter, we are here.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: July 2026

The Golden Hour After an Injury

Trauma is the leading cause of death for Americans under 45, and the first hour after a serious injury decides more than any other. Rapid evaluation and stabilization in that window is what trauma care is built around.

Texas classifies trauma facilities into four levels under Health and Safety Code Chapter 254. Our role in that system is honest and specific: we are the fast entry point for assessment, imaging, bleeding control and stabilization in this part of North Texas.

Most everyday injuries finish here. Injuries that need operative surgery or ICU care are stabilized first, then transferred directly to a Level I or II trauma center with the workup already done.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: July 2026

Injury Signs That Need the ER Now

The first two mean call 911 and do not move the person. For the rest, come straight in while someone else drives.

Unconscious After Impact

Any loss of consciousness after a crash or fall is a 911 call. Do not move them.

Severe or Spurting Bleeding

Blood that spurts or will not stop with direct pressure. Press hard and call 911.

Possible Neck or Back Injury

Severe neck or back pain after impact needs spinal precautions. Keep the person still.

Chest Pain After a Crash

Blunt chest impact can bruise the heart or collapse a lung. Get checked today.

Belly Pain After Blunt Impact

Internal bleeding can hide behind a seatbelt bruise. Same-day imaging settles it.

Deformity or Suspected Break

A limb that looks wrong, will not bear weight, or has bone visible.

Numbness or Weakness

Loss of feeling or strength in any limb after an injury points to nerve involvement.

Worsening Headache, Vomiting

After any head impact, a building headache or repeated vomiting needs a CT scan.

What Happens the Moment You Arrive

Trauma care follows the same disciplined survey everywhere in the world. Ours starts at the door.

1. ABCDE Survey First

Airway, breathing, circulation, neuro status and full exposure, with spine precautions until cleared.

2. Imaging That Finds It All

CT from head to pelvis, X-rays for fractures, and bedside ultrasound for internal bleeding.

3. Stop, Splint, Stitch

Bleeding control, deep laceration repair, tetanus update, fracture splinting and IV pain relief.

4. Treat Here or Transfer

Most injuries finish here. Operative trauma is stabilized and moved to a Level I or II center.

Built for Irving's Roads and Worksites

Three corridors send us most of our crash patients: Hwy 114 and 183 through Las Colinas with their high-speed merges, the stop-and-go chain collisions on I-635, and the fast stretches of SH 161. Falls in older adults and Las Colinas worksite injuries round out the list. Our Hwy 114/183 car-accident guide covers the corridor patterns in detail.

Recovery is planned before you leave: orthopedic follow-up within a week for a fracture, concussion clearance for any head injury, and blood clot prevention guidance for anyone immobilized afterward.

You also leave with documentation: a complete ER record that supports your insurance or legal claim, plus a mental health check-in, because post-crash stress is real and treatable.

911, ER, or Wait and Watch?

After a crash, adrenaline is a bad advisor. Here is the honest split.

Call 911

Unconsciousness, uncontrolled bleeding, possible spine injury, a rollover or ejection, or a struck pedestrian or cyclist. Do not move them.

Come to the ER

Alert and stable with a suspected break, a deep cut, chest or belly pain after impact, or a head hit with symptoms. Someone else drives.

Feel Fine? Still Consider It

Adrenaline masks pain for hours, and whiplash and internal bleeding declare themselves over 24 to 48 hours. A same-day exam creates the baseline that protects you.

Trauma and Car Accident Questions, Answered

Can a freestanding ER handle a car accident?

Yes. Texas freestanding emergency facilities are licensed for initial trauma assessment, imaging, bleeding control, fracture stabilization and resuscitation. For most everyday crashes the entire workup finishes here. When operative surgery is needed, we stabilize first and transfer with the imaging already done.

Will my auto insurance pay for an ER visit after a crash?

Texas auto policies often include MedPay or Personal Injury Protection that covers medical bills regardless of fault, and the federal No Surprises Act protects you from balance billing for emergency care. Bring your auto policy details and we can discuss coverage on arrival.

Do I need an ER visit if I feel fine after a low-speed crash?

Often, yes. Whiplash, contusions and even internal bleeding can take 24 to 48 hours to show themselves, and adrenaline masks pain in the first hours. A same-day evaluation creates a documented baseline that protects both your health and any later claim.

Do you treat children after accidents?

Yes. Pediatric trauma is evaluated with age-appropriate tools and equipment sized for children. When subspecialty pediatric trauma surgery is required, we coordinate direct transfer to Children’s Health Dallas or Cook Children’s in Fort Worth.

What happens after the ER visit?

Recovery is mapped before discharge: orthopedic follow-up for fractures, a concussion-clearance protocol for head injuries, physical therapy referrals for soft-tissue damage, blood clot prevention guidance if you will be immobilized, and a copy of your record for insurance.

Will my insurance cover an ER trauma visit?

Emergency care is protected. Under the federal No Surprises Act and Texas Department of Insurance balance-billing rules, patients are shielded from surprise balance bills for emergency treatment. We post all required Texas disclosures and can discuss costs with you on arrival.

The First Hour Decides the Next Year

Imaging, stabilization and straight answers after any injury. Call 911 when it is serious. Walk in 24/7 for everything else.

content.raw:
TL;DR: Heat stroke is the most serious heat-related illness. A core body temperature above 104 F (40 C) damages brain, kidney, and muscle tissue within minutes. Call 911 if a person is confused, unconscious, or has hot skin and rapid pulse after sun or heat exposure. ER of Irving is open 24/7 with cold-water immersion or evaporative cooling, IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and rhabdomyolysis monitoring.

What Is Heat Stroke?

Heat stroke happens when the body's temperature-regulation system fails. Sweating stops being effective, core temperature climbs past 104 F, and organs begin to fail. Without rapid cooling, heat stroke can cause seizures, kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), and death.

Per the CDC heat-illness page, heat stroke is the most serious illness on the heat spectrum, which also includes heat cramps, heat syncope, and heat exhaustion. Heat stroke can occur from environmental exposure (classic) or vigorous exertion in hot weather (exertional, common in athletes, soldiers, and outdoor workers).

Heat Stroke vs Heat Exhaustion: The Critical Differential

FeatureHeat ExhaustionHeat Stroke
Core temperatureLess than 104 F104 F or higher
SkinCool, pale, sweatyHot, dry (classic) or sweaty (exertional)
Mental statusTired, may have headacheConfused, irritable, seizing, or unconscious
PulseFast, weakFast, strong
TreatmentMove to cool area, oral fluids911, rapid cooling, ER

The defining feature is mental-status change. Confusion, slurred speech, or unconsciousness in a hot person is heat stroke until proven otherwise. For background, see our Heat Stroke vs Heat Exhaustion guide.

Heat Stroke Warning Signs

  • Core body temperature 104 F (40 C) or higher
  • Confusion, agitation, slurred speech, irritability, or sudden behavior change
  • Seizures
  • Loss of consciousness
  • Hot, dry skin (classic heat stroke) or profuse sweating (exertional heat stroke)
  • Rapid, strong pulse
  • Headache, nausea, vomiting
  • Rapid, shallow breathing

Heat stroke is one of the few medical emergencies where cooling comes before transport. Every minute the core temperature stays above 104 F adds to organ damage.

Who Is at Highest Risk?

  • Adults age 65 and older
  • Infants and young children left in cars or unconditioned spaces
  • Outdoor workers (roofing, construction, landscaping, agriculture)
  • High school and college athletes during August practices
  • People with chronic heart, lung, or kidney disease
  • People taking diuretics, beta-blockers, antihistamines, or stimulant medications
  • Anyone using alcohol or recreational drugs in hot conditions
  • People without access to air conditioning during a heat advisory

Why Texas Summer Is Different

The Dallas-Fort Worth heat index regularly climbs past 105 F from June through early September. North Texas humidity adds to the load: when the air is already saturated, sweat does not evaporate, so the body cannot shed heat. Outdoor workers in Las Colinas, Grand Prairie, and Arlington face the longest exposure windows.

For Texas-specific workplace heat-illness data, see NIOSH heat-stress resources. For Las Colinas workplace presentations, see our Workplace Injuries guide.

How ER of Irving Treats Heat Stroke

Heat stroke treatment is structured and time-critical:

  1. Rapid cooling. The single most important intervention. We use cold-water immersion (preferred for exertional heat stroke), evaporative cooling with mist and fans, and ice packs to neck, axillae, and groin until core temperature reaches 102 F.
  2. Continuous core temperature monitoring with rectal or esophageal probe (skin and oral readings are unreliable in heat stroke).
  3. IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline. See our Dehydration Treatment page for the broader fluid-resuscitation context.
  4. Electrolyte correction for sodium, potassium, calcium, and phosphate disturbances.
  5. Rhabdomyolysis workup. Creatine kinase (CK), urine myoglobin, kidney function. Aggressive IV fluids if rhabdomyolysis is confirmed.
  6. Seizure control with benzodiazepines if needed.
  7. Airway support for severe altered mental status.
  8. ICU or hospital transfer for moderate-to-severe cases. We coordinate the next step.

First Aid Before the ER Arrives

While waiting for EMS:

  • Move the person out of the sun and into the coolest available space
  • Remove excess clothing
  • Spray with cool water or apply wet towels, ice packs, or a cold-water bath if available
  • Direct a fan at the person to encourage evaporation
  • Do not give fluids by mouth if the person is confused or unconscious (aspiration risk)
  • Roll an unconscious person onto their side
  • Note the time symptoms started so the ER team can estimate exposure duration

When to Call 911 vs Drive

Call 911 for any of the following:

  • Confusion, slurred speech, or unconsciousness during or after heat exposure
  • Body temperature 104 F or above
  • Seizures
  • Hot skin paired with rapid pulse and headache
  • An athlete who collapses in practice or a game
  • A child or adult discovered unresponsive in a hot car

Driving to the ER is reasonable only if symptoms are mild (heavy sweating, headache, fatigue, normal mental status) and someone else can drive.

Preventing Heat Stroke

  • Drink water on a schedule, not just when thirsty. Aim for 16 to 32 ounces per hour during outdoor work or exercise in hot weather.
  • Add electrolytes during prolonged exertion. Water alone for 3 to 4 hours can cause dangerously low sodium.
  • Schedule outdoor work and exercise for early morning or evening.
  • Wear light-colored, loose-fitting clothing and a wide-brim hat.
  • Take shade breaks every 20 to 30 minutes in extreme heat.
  • Never leave a child, elderly person, or pet in a parked car, even for a minute.
  • Check on elderly neighbors and family during heat advisories, especially anyone without air conditioning.
  • Athletes should acclimatize over 10 to 14 days at the start of summer practice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can heat stroke happen indoors?

Yes. Classic heat stroke is common during heat waves in unconditioned homes, particularly for elderly people, infants, and people without working air conditioning. Indoor heat stroke can develop over days as the body loses the ability to compensate.

What is the difference between exertional and classic heat stroke?

Exertional heat stroke happens during intense physical activity, often in athletes or laborers, and often involves profuse sweating. Classic heat stroke happens to vulnerable people during ambient heat waves and often involves dry skin. The treatment is the same: rapid cooling first.

How fast can heat stroke kill?

Without cooling, heat stroke can be fatal within an hour. The longer the core temperature stays above 104 F, the higher the risk of permanent organ damage and death.

What is rhabdomyolysis and why does it matter after heat stroke?

Rhabdomyolysis is the breakdown of muscle tissue that releases proteins into the bloodstream, where they can clog the kidneys. It is a common complication of exertional heat stroke and a major reason patients need ER-level monitoring rather than home cooling.

Will my insurance cover an ER heat stroke visit?

ER of Irving is a Texas-licensed freestanding emergency medical care facility. Per the federal No Surprises Act and Texas Department of Insurance balance-billing rules, patients are protected from balance billing for emergency care. We post all required disclosures under Texas H&S Code Chapter 254 and can discuss costs with you on arrival.

Visit ER of Irving for 24/7 Heat Stroke Emergency Care

Heat stroke is one of the few medical emergencies where every minute of cooling buys back organ function. ER of Irving is open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, equipped with cold-water immersion, IV resuscitation, continuous core-temperature monitoring, and direct ICU coordination for severe cases.

For symptom-stage detail and the heat-illness spectrum, see our Heat Stroke vs Heat Exhaustion guide. For the broader hydration framework, see our Dehydration Treatment service page and Signs of Dehydration guide. For non-emergency questions, use our Contact Us form. When the Texas sun hits hard, we are here.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: July 2026

24/7 Emergency Room in Irving, TX

Heat Stroke Emergency Treatment in Irving, TX

A core temperature above 104 damages organs within minutes, and Texas summers deliver it. Rapid cooling, IV fluids and core monitoring, 24/7.

Call (972) 893-3148 Now
Get Directions

What Is Heat Stroke?

Heat stroke is what happens when the body’s cooling system fails. Sweating stops working, core temperature climbs past 104, and the brain, kidneys and muscles start taking damage. Per the CDC, it is the most serious illness on the heat spectrum.

It comes in two forms. Classic heat stroke strikes vulnerable people during heat waves, often indoors without air conditioning, and the skin turns hot and dry. Exertional heat stroke hits athletes and outdoor workers mid-effort, often while still sweating heavily.

The tell is the mind: confusion, slurred speech, or collapse in a hot person is heat stroke until proven otherwise.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: July 2026

Heat Stroke Warning Signs

The first two mean call 911 and start cooling on the spot. Heat stroke is one of the few emergencies where cooling comes before transport.

Confusion in the Heat

Confusion, slurred speech, or odd behavior in a hot person is heat stroke until proven otherwise. Call 911.

Passed Out or Seizing

Collapse or a seizure during heat exposure is a 911 emergency. Start cooling while you wait.

Temperature of 104 or More

The threshold where organ damage begins, and every minute above it counts.

Hot, Dry Skin

Sweating has failed. Athletes with exertional heat stroke may still be drenched.

Racing, Pounding Pulse

A fast, strong pulse as the heart works overtime to shed heat.

Pounding Headache, Nausea

A severe headache with nausea or vomiting after sun or heat exposure.

An Athlete Down in Practice

August two-a-days are prime time for exertional heat stroke. Cool first, transport second.

Found in a Hot Car or Home

Children, older adults, and anyone without air conditioning during a heat advisory.

What Happens the Moment You Arrive

The protocol has one priority: get the core temperature down, fast.

1. Cooling Before Everything

Cold-water immersion, mist and fans, and ice to the neck and groin until the core reaches 102.

2. True Core Temperature

A core probe, because skin and oral readings lie during heat stroke.

3. IV Fluids and Electrolytes

Saline resuscitation, with sodium, potassium and calcium corrected as labs return.

4. Muscle and Kidney Watch

Labs catch muscle breakdown before it clogs the kidneys, with ICU coordination for severe cases.

Cooling Comes Before Transport

While waiting for EMS: move the person to the coolest space available, strip excess clothing, soak them with cool water or wet towels, and aim a fan at them. Roll an unconscious person onto their side, and never give fluids by mouth to someone confused.

North Texas earns this page. The DFW heat index tops 105 from June to September, and humidity keeps sweat from evaporating, so the body cannot shed heat. Outdoor workers and August athletes carry the highest risk, and prevention is unglamorous but real: water on a schedule, electrolytes during long efforts, morning work hours, and 10 to 14 days of acclimatization.

Milder heat illness overlaps with dehydration, and our heat stroke vs heat exhaustion guide walks the full spectrum.

911, ER, or Shade and Water?

Judge by the mind and the thermometer, not by how tough the person usually is.

Call 911 and Cool

Confusion, collapse, seizures, or a temperature at 104 and climbing. Start cooling on the spot; every minute above 104 costs organ function.

Come to the ER

Heavy sweating with headache, cramps and exhaustion that do not improve within 30 minutes of shade and fluids. That is heat exhaustion sliding toward trouble.

Cool Down at Home

Mild cramps or fatigue with clear thinking: shade, water with electrolytes, and rest. Improvement should be obvious within the hour.

Heat Stroke Questions, Answered

What is the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke?

Heat exhaustion means cool, sweaty skin, fatigue and headache with a clear mind, and it responds to shade and fluids. Heat stroke means a core temperature of 104 or higher with confusion, seizures, or unconsciousness. The mental status change is the line: once thinking changes, call 911.

Can heat stroke happen indoors?

Yes. Classic heat stroke is common during heat waves in homes without working air conditioning, especially for older adults and infants. It can build over days as the body slowly loses the ability to compensate. Check on elderly neighbors during heat advisories.

How fast can heat stroke kill?

Without cooling, heat stroke can be fatal within an hour, and every minute the core stays above 104 adds organ damage. That is why cooling starts immediately, on the field or in the driveway, before and during transport.

What is rhabdomyolysis and why does it matter?

Rhabdomyolysis is muscle tissue breaking down and releasing proteins that clog the kidneys. It is a common complication of exertional heat stroke and the main reason a collapsed athlete needs ER-level labs and IV fluids rather than a cool-down on the sidelines.

How do I prevent heat stroke working outside in Texas?

Drink 16 to 32 ounces of water per hour on a schedule, add electrolytes past the second hour, take shade breaks every 20 to 30 minutes, and shift heavy work to morning. New workers and early-season athletes need 10 to 14 days to acclimatize. And never leave anyone in a parked car.

Will insurance cover an ER heat stroke visit?

Emergency care is protected. Under the federal No Surprises Act and Texas Department of Insurance balance-billing rules, patients are shielded from surprise balance bills for emergency treatment. We post all required Texas disclosures and can discuss costs with you on arrival.

Every Minute of Cooling Buys Back Organ Function

Cold-water immersion, IV fluids and continuous core monitoring, all summer long. Call 911 for confusion or collapse. We are here 24/7.

Call (972) 893-3148
Get Directions

content.raw:
TL;DR: Anaphylaxis is a severe, whole-body allergic reaction that can kill within minutes. Use your epinephrine auto-injector first, then call 911. Even if symptoms improve, a biphasic (second-wave) reaction can occur 1 to 8 hours later. Visit ER of Irving for monitored observation, IV fluids, airway support, and follow-up medication. We are open 24 hours a day.

What Is Anaphylaxis?

Anaphylaxis is a severe, generalized allergic reaction that affects two or more body systems at the same time. The immune system overreacts to a trigger, releasing chemicals (mainly histamine) that cause blood vessels to leak, airways to swell, and blood pressure to drop. Without rapid treatment, anaphylaxis can lead to airway closure, shock, and death.

An estimated 45,000 to 50,000 anaphylaxis-related emergency-room visits happen each year in the United States, and ED visits for anaphylaxis have more than doubled from 2008 to 2016. Food, medications, and insect stings are the three biggest triggers.

8 Anaphylaxis Warning Signs by Body System

Anaphylaxis usually involves at least two of the body systems below within minutes to a few hours of exposure.

  • Skin: hives, flushing, severe itching, swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat
  • Airway: tightness in the throat, hoarse voice, trouble swallowing, wheezing, shortness of breath
  • Cardiovascular: rapid pulse, dizziness, fainting, low blood pressure, pale or sweaty skin
  • Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea
  • Neurological: sense of impending doom, confusion, loss of consciousness
  • Combination patterns: hives plus wheezing, or vomiting plus low blood pressure

For background on what an unexplained skin reaction may signal before it escalates, see our Rashes Treatment service page.

Common Anaphylaxis Triggers

Trigger ClassCommon ExamplesTypical Onset
FoodPeanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, milk, eggs, sesame, wheat, soyMinutes to 1 hour
MedicationsPenicillin, sulfa drugs, NSAIDs, contrast dye, biologicsMinutes to 1 hour
Insect venomBees, wasps, hornets, yellow jackets, fire antsMinutes
LatexGloves, balloons, dental dam, urinary cathetersMinutes to hours
Exercise-inducedVigorous exercise within 4 hours of trigger food (often wheat)During or shortly after exercise
IdiopathicNo identifiable triggerVariable

Why You Cannot Skip the ER After EpiPen Use

Epinephrine is the first and most important treatment for anaphylaxis. It reverses airway swelling, raises blood pressure, and stops the cascade. But it is not the end of treatment.

Up to 20 percent of anaphylaxis cases involve a biphasic reaction: a second wave of symptoms that returns 1 to 8 hours after the initial reaction settles. This can happen even when the first dose of epinephrine seemed to work perfectly. Without monitoring, the second reaction can be fatal.

ER of Irving keeps post-epinephrine patients under observation for the recommended window, with IV access, continuous monitoring, and additional doses of epinephrine ready if symptoms return. For a deeper guide on the EpiPen recovery period, see our Anaphylaxis Recovery blog.

How ER of Irving Treats Anaphylaxis

Once anaphylaxis is recognized, our protocol moves in minutes:

  1. Intramuscular epinephrine as first-line treatment (not IV, not subcutaneous). Repeat every 5 to 15 minutes if symptoms persist.
  2. Airway management. Oxygen, positioning, and intubation readiness if airway swelling is significant.
  3. IV access and fluid resuscitation. Crystalloid boluses for hypotension.
  4. Adjunct medications. H1 and H2 antihistamines, corticosteroids, and inhaled bronchodilators for residual wheezing.
  5. Vasopressors. For shock that does not respond to fluids and epinephrine.
  6. Monitored observation per current guidelines (typically several hours; longer if the reaction was severe, required multiple epinephrine doses, or involved asthma).
  7. Discharge plan. Two epinephrine auto-injector prescriptions, allergist referral, written anaphylaxis action plan, and trigger-avoidance counseling.

Anaphylaxis vs Mild Allergic Reaction

FeatureMild Allergic ReactionAnaphylaxis
Body systems involvedOne (usually skin)Two or more
HivesLocal or scatteredWidespread, with other symptoms
BreathingNormalWheezing, tightness, stridor
ThroatMild itchTightness, hoarseness, swelling
Blood pressureNormalLow, dizzy, faint
First-line treatmentOral antihistamineIM epinephrine + 911
DispositionHome with monitoringER observation

When in doubt, use the EpiPen. Epinephrine causes minimal harm in someone who turns out to have had a milder reaction. Withholding it from someone in true anaphylaxis can be fatal.

Living with Severe Allergies

After a confirmed anaphylaxis episode, the goal shifts to preventing the next one. Standard follow-up includes:

  • Allergist evaluation with specific IgE testing or skin prick testing to confirm triggers
  • Two epinephrine auto-injectors carried at all times (school, work, travel)
  • Written anaphylaxis action plan signed by your clinician
  • Medical alert ID bracelet or wallet card
  • Trigger-avoidance education for family members, teachers, coaches, restaurants
  • For severe insect-venom allergy: discussion of venom immunotherapy with an allergist
  • For peanut and other food allergies: consideration of FDA-approved oral immunotherapy when appropriate

When to Call 911 vs Drive to the ER

Call 911 immediately for any of the following:

  • Trouble breathing or swallowing after exposure to a known or suspected trigger
  • Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat
  • Hives plus dizziness, vomiting, or low blood pressure
  • Sudden loss of consciousness
  • Symptoms returning after an EpiPen seemed to work

EMS can give additional epinephrine in the field, secure the airway, and transmit vitals ahead. Driving yourself is not safe during an active anaphylactic reaction.

Frequently Asked Questions

If the EpiPen worked, do I still need the ER?

Yes. The biphasic reaction risk (up to 1 in 5 cases) means symptoms can return hours later even if the first dose seemed to fix everything. ER observation catches the rebound before it becomes airway closure.

How long does an EpiPen last in my system?

Epinephrine wears off within 10 to 20 minutes. That is why a second dose is often needed and why ER monitoring matters.

Can anaphylaxis happen on first exposure to a trigger?

Usually anaphylaxis requires prior sensitization, meaning the immune system has met the trigger before. With insect stings and some medications, however, the prior exposure may have been so mild it went unnoticed.

Can I use an expired EpiPen if it is all I have?

Yes, in an emergency. An expired EpiPen still delivers most of its epinephrine and is better than nothing. Use it, then replace the auto-injector after the event.

TL;DR: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to infection that can kill within hours. Warning signs include high fever or low body temperature, fast heart rate, fast breathing, confusion, severe pain, and clammy skin. Each hour of delay raises the risk of death by 4 to 9 percent. Call 911 or visit ER of Irving immediately. Our 24/7 emergency facility runs the standard sepsis one-hour bundle: lactate, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and IV fluid resuscitation.

What Is Sepsis?

Sepsis is the body's extreme response to an infection. The immune system stops fighting only the invading germ and starts damaging its own tissues and organs. Left untreated, sepsis progresses to septic shock, where blood pressure crashes and organ failure follows.

According to the CDC, at least 1.7 million American adults develop sepsis each year and at least 350,000 die from it. Sepsis is the third-leading cause of death in U.S. hospitals.

Any infection can trigger sepsis. The most common sources are pneumonia, urinary tract infections (often from kidney stones or catheters), abdominal infections like appendicitis, and skin infections.

Sepsis Warning Signs You Should Not Ignore

The CDC promotes the simple "TIME" acronym for sepsis recognition:

  • T - Temperature higher than normal or lower than normal
  • I - Infection known or suspected, including new wound, urinary symptoms, cough, recent surgery
  • M - Mental decline: confusion, sleepy, hard to rouse
  • E - Extremely ill: severe pain or discomfort, "I feel like I might die"

Other red-flag findings often present in early sepsis:

  • Heart rate above 90 beats per minute
  • Breathing rate above 22 breaths per minute or shortness of breath
  • Blood pressure dropping when standing
  • Cold, clammy, or mottled skin
  • Less urine output than normal
  • Skin rash that does not blanch when pressed

If you have an infection and any two of the above signs, treat it as sepsis until proven otherwise.

Who Is at Higher Risk for Sepsis?

Per the NIH NIGMS sepsis fact sheet, the highest-risk groups include:

  • Adults 65 and older
  • Children younger than 1 year
  • People with chronic conditions like diabetes, lung disease, cancer, or kidney disease
  • People with weakened immune systems (chemotherapy, transplant, HIV, biologic medications)
  • Recent hospitalization or invasive procedure
  • People with indwelling lines, catheters, or feeding tubes
  • Pregnant or recently postpartum women
  • Anyone with severe burns or major wounds

Why Every Hour Matters: The Sepsis One-Hour Bundle

For sepsis, time is organ function. Each hour of delay before antibiotic administration increases the mortality risk by an estimated 4 to 9 percent. The international Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends a one-hour bundle: lactate measurement, blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, all started within 60 minutes of recognition.

ER of Irving runs this bundle on every suspected sepsis case. Our on-site lab returns lactate and basic chemistry in under 20 minutes. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are stocked and ready to deliver at the bedside.

Common Infection Sources That Lead to Sepsis

SourceSuggesting SymptomsCommon Population
PneumoniaCough, fever, fast breathing, chest painOlder adults, smokers, post-flu
Urinary tract infectionBurning urination, flank pain, feverWomen, catheter users, kidney stone patients
Abdominal infectionSevere abdominal pain, vomiting, feverAppendicitis, diverticulitis, perforation
Skin or wound infectionSpreading redness, pus, warmthDiabetics, post-surgical, IV drug users
Catheter or line infectionRedness at line site, fever with no other sourceDialysis, chemotherapy, ICU recovery
Postpartum infectionFever, foul lochia, pelvic painRecent vaginal or C-section delivery

Pneumonia is the single most common sepsis trigger in U.S. adults, followed by UTIs. Skin and intra-abdominal sources account for most of the rest.

How ER of Irving Treats Suspected Sepsis

Once sepsis is suspected, our protocol moves quickly:

  1. Triage within minutes. qSOFA scoring (respiratory rate, mental status, blood pressure) at the door.
  2. Lactate level. A point-of-care or stat lab result within 20 minutes. A lactate above 2 mmol/L confirms early tissue hypoperfusion.
  3. Blood cultures drawn before antibiotics, when feasible.
  4. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 60 minutes of recognition.
  5. IV fluid resuscitation. 30 mL per kg of crystalloid fluid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L.
  6. Source control workup. Chest X-ray, urinalysis, CT scan, or wound exam to find the underlying infection.
  7. Vasopressors if blood pressure stays low after fluids.
  8. ICU coordination and transfer for moderate-to-severe cases. We arrange the next step.

Sepsis vs Flu vs Common Cold: How to Tell the Difference

FeatureCommon ColdInfluenzaSepsis
FeverRare or low-gradeOften 102 F or higherVery high or unusually low
Heart rateNormalMildly elevatedAbove 90, often above 110
Mental statusClearTired but clearConfused, sleepy, hard to rouse
SkinNormalFlushedClammy, mottled, or rash
Speed of declineSlow, days1 to 2 daysHours
ActionRest, fluidsAntivirals, monitorCall 911 or ER now

The hallmark of sepsis is rapid systemic decline despite the underlying infection seeming "ordinary." If a person with the flu becomes confused, breathless, or unable to stand, treat it as sepsis until cleared.

When to Call 911 vs Drive to the ER

Call 911 immediately if a person with a known or suspected infection shows any of the following:

  • Confusion or marked drop in alertness
  • Fast or labored breathing
  • Faintness or collapse on standing
  • Skin that is mottled, cold, or has a non-blanching rash
  • Very high or very low body temperature
  • Severe pain described as the worst of their life

EMS can start oxygen and IV access in the field, transmit vitals ahead, and shave minutes off door-to-antibiotic time. Driving yourself is acceptable only if symptoms are mild and stable and someone else can drive.

Post-Sepsis Syndrome: Recovery After the ER

Surviving sepsis is only the first step. Up to half of sepsis survivors experience post-sepsis syndrome: persistent fatigue, difficulty sleeping, weakness, joint or muscle pain, cognitive changes, anxiety, or depression that can last months or years.

Follow-up steps after a sepsis ER visit usually include:

  • Primary care visit within 1 week of discharge
  • Medication review (especially if antibiotics or vasopressors changed your usual regimen)
  • Physical or occupational therapy when deconditioning is significant
  • Mental health check, since post-sepsis depression and PTSD are common
  • Vaccination review (flu, pneumococcal, COVID, RSV depending on age and risk)

Frequently Asked Questions

Can sepsis happen from a small cut or insect bite?

Yes. Any infection can seed sepsis, including a minor skin infection, an infected ingrown toenail, an animal or insect bite, or a UTI that was previously mild. The body's response, not the size of the wound, determines whether sepsis develops.

What is the difference between sepsis and septicemia?

Septicemia is an older term that means bacteria in the bloodstream. Sepsis is the body's systemic response to that infection. Sepsis can occur with or without bacteria proven in the blood, and it is the more clinically meaningful term today.

How quickly can sepsis kill?

Severe sepsis can progress to septic shock and death within hours. This is why the one-hour antibiotic bundle exists. Do not "wait until morning" if you suspect sepsis.

Will my vital signs always be abnormal in early sepsis?

Not always. Older adults and immunocompromised people may present with subtle findings, including a body temperature lower than normal rather than higher. Confusion, weakness, or "just not acting right" in an elderly person with a recent infection should be evaluated as a possible sepsis case.

Will my insurance cover an ER sepsis visit?

content.raw:
TL;DR: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening complication of diabetes that can develop in under 24 hours. Warning signs include very high blood sugar, fruity-smelling breath, deep rapid breathing, vomiting, abdominal pain, and confusion. Call 911 or visit ER of Irving immediately. Our 24/7 emergency facility manages DKA with IV fluids, insulin, electrolyte monitoring, and infection workup.

What Is Diabetic Ketoacidosis?

Diabetic ketoacidosis happens when the body cannot use sugar (glucose) for energy because of an insulin shortage. Cells start burning fat instead, releasing acidic byproducts called ketones. The blood becomes acidic, blood sugar climbs, and the body dehydrates rapidly.

According to a CDC MMWR report, the U.S. DKA hospitalization rate has been climbing since 2009, with more than 220,000 DKA admissions per year by 2017. DKA is most common in people with type 1 diabetes but can also occur in type 2 diabetes during severe illness or stress.

8 Warning Signs of Diabetic Ketoacidosis

Per the National Library of Medicine, DKA usually develops over 24 hours and presents with:

  • Excessive thirst (polydipsia) that does not go away no matter how much you drink
  • Frequent urination (polyuria), often through the night
  • Very high blood sugar (typically above 250 mg/dL on a home glucometer)
  • Nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain that mimics a stomach virus
  • Fruity-smelling breath (acetone) caused by ketones leaving through the lungs
  • Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul respirations) as the body tries to blow off acid
  • Fatigue, weakness, and muscle aches
  • Confusion, drowsiness, or difficulty staying awake in advanced cases

For a deeper dive on each symptom and what it means physiologically, see our companion guide on recognizing a sugar emergency.

Who Is at Risk for DKA?

DKA is most often the first sign of type 1 diabetes in a previously healthy person. It can also strike people with diagnosed diabetes, especially when:

  • An insulin dose is missed or an insulin pump malfunctions
  • A serious infection (pneumonia, UTI, sepsis) raises insulin demand
  • A heart attack, stroke, or trauma triggers a stress response
  • SGLT2-inhibitor medications are taken with reduced food or fluid intake (euglycemic DKA, where blood sugar can be near normal but ketones are still high)
  • Alcohol use, pregnancy, or recent surgery disrupts blood sugar control
  • Steroid medications increase blood sugar

Common DKA Triggers

About half of all DKA admissions trace back to a missed insulin dose or an infection. Other common triggers include a malfunctioning insulin pump, a newly diagnosed case of diabetes, severe dehydration in hot weather, or eating disorders that lead to insulin omission.

How ER of Irving Treats DKA

DKA care is time-critical and follows a structured ER protocol:

  1. Rapid vitals and triage within minutes of arrival.
  2. Blood work. Glucose, electrolytes, anion gap, venous blood gas, ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate), kidney function, complete blood count.
  3. Urine analysis. Ketones, glucose, signs of infection.
  4. EKG to screen for low or high potassium and possible cardiac triggers.
  5. IV fluid resuscitation. Normal saline corrects dehydration and starts to lower blood sugar.
  6. IV insulin infusion. Continuous low-dose insulin closes the ketone gap and brings blood sugar down safely.
  7. Potassium replacement. Insulin shifts potassium into cells. Replacement prevents dangerous heart-rhythm complications.
  8. Infection workup. Chest X-ray, urinalysis, blood cultures if fever, white-cell count, or other signs suggest infection.
  9. Coordinated admission or transfer. Most DKA patients need ICU or stepdown unit monitoring. We coordinate the next step.

DKA vs HHS: How They Differ

Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) is the type 2 diabetic emergency cousin of DKA. The two conditions share many features but differ in important ways.

FeatureDKAHHS
Most common diabetes typeType 1 (also type 2 in stress)Type 2
Blood sugarAbove 250 mg/dLAbove 600 mg/dL
KetonesHighMinimal or absent
AcidosisYesNo or mild
OnsetHours to a dayDays to weeks
Mental statusMostly preserved earlyMore commonly altered
MortalityAbout 0.4% (rising in ICU)5% to 20%

The treatments overlap (IV fluids, insulin, electrolyte replacement) but the pace and target endpoints differ. Our ER team identifies which condition applies within the first hour.

When to Call 911 vs Drive to the ER

Call 911, do not drive yourself, if you experience:

  • Confusion, severe drowsiness, or inability to stay awake
  • Fast deep breathing or shortness of breath
  • Persistent vomiting and inability to keep fluids down
  • Chest pain or palpitations in someone with diabetes
  • A blood sugar reading above 300 mg/dL with any of the above
  • A child with diabetes who appears suddenly limp, sleepy, or unable to focus

If symptoms are mild (high sugar, some thirst, mild nausea) and you can keep fluids down, you may walk in to ER of Irving instead of calling 911. Bring your glucometer, recent ketone readings, and a list of your medications.

Long-Term Care After a DKA Episode

Recovery does not stop when the IV insulin drip ends. After a DKA episode, expect:

  • Endocrinology follow-up within 1 to 2 weeks
  • A diabetes-educator session to review insulin technique, pump settings, or sick-day rules
  • Continuous glucose monitor (CGM) consideration if you do not already use one
  • An honest review of what triggered the episode so a repeat is less likely

Recurrent DKA is common when triggers are not addressed. About 1 in 5 patients are back in the ER within a year. The follow-up visit is as important as the ER visit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can DKA happen if I do not have diabetes?

Yes. DKA can be the first presentation of previously undiagnosed type 1 diabetes, especially in children, teens, and young adults. Symptoms usually include weight loss, intense thirst, and frequent urination for days before the crisis.

How fast does DKA progress?

DKA usually develops over 24 hours but can move from mild to severe within 6 to 12 hours, especially if vomiting prevents fluid intake. Do not assume you have more time than you do.

Can DKA be prevented at home with extra insulin?

Sometimes. People with established diabetes should follow their sick-day rules (check sugars and ketones every 2 to 4 hours, take correction doses, and stay hydrated). Once vomiting starts or ketones climb, home management is no longer safe.

Is DKA fatal?

Modern in-hospital DKA mortality is around 0.4%, but it climbs when the episode is severe, the patient is elderly, or there is an underlying infection or heart event. ICU-level DKA care has been increasing in the United States, signaling that more severe cases are reaching the hospital.

Does insurance cover ER DKA care?

Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) Emergency Treatment in Irving, TX

Blood sugar over 250, fruity breath, deep rapid breathing, or vomiting with diabetes? DKA can turn severe in hours. IV insulin and fluids start immediately.

Call (972) 893-3148 Now
Get Directions

What Is Diabetic Ketoacidosis?

DKA happens when the body runs short on insulin and cannot use sugar for energy. Cells burn fat instead, releasing acids called ketones. Blood sugar climbs, the blood turns acidic, and the body dehydrates fast.

According to a CDC report, DKA hospitalizations have climbed past 220,000 per year in the United States. It is most common in type 1 diabetes, but type 2 diabetics can develop it during serious illness or stress.

The whole crisis can build in under 24 hours, and once vomiting starts it accelerates. That is why DKA is an emergency room problem, not a wait-and-see one.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: July 2026

DKA Warning Signs

The first two mean call 911. The rest, checked together with a glucometer, mean come in now.

Confusion or Hard to Wake

Drowsiness, confusion, or trouble staying awake is advanced DKA. Call 911.

Deep, Rapid Breathing

The body blowing off acid through fast, deep breaths is late-stage DKA. Call 911.

Thirst That Will Not Quit

Drinking constantly and staying thirsty anyway, often with a dry mouth.

Urinating Around the Clock

Frequent bathroom trips, especially through the night, as sugar pulls water out.

Sugar Above 250

A home glucometer reading over 250 mg/dL that correction doses will not bring down.

Nausea or Belly Pain

DKA often mimics a stomach virus. In a diabetic, do not assume it is one.

Fruity-Smelling Breath

Acetone leaving through the lungs. A classic ketone sign others may notice first.

Weakness and Muscle Aches

Deep fatigue and aching muscles as the body runs on the wrong fuel.

What Happens the Moment You Arrive

DKA care is time-critical and follows a structured protocol from the first minutes.

1. Vitals and Labs Fast

Glucose, ketones, electrolytes and blood gas drawn within minutes, plus an EKG for potassium.

2. IV Fluids First

Saline corrects the dehydration and starts lowering blood sugar on its own.

3. IV Insulin Drip

Continuous low-dose insulin closes the ketone gap safely, with potassium replaced as it shifts.

4. Find the Trigger

Infection workup and medication review, then coordinated ICU or endocrine admission when needed.

Why DKA Cannot Be Fixed at Home

Diabetics with sick-day rules can manage mild high sugars: check glucose and ketones every 2 to 4 hours, take correction doses, and push fluids. The moment vomiting starts or ketones keep climbing, home management stops being safe.

Two traps catch people off guard. SGLT2-inhibitor medications can cause DKA with near-normal blood sugar, so ketones matter more than the glucometer. And type 2 diabetics can develop HHS, a slower cousin with sugars above 600 and higher mortality. We tell the two apart within the first hour.

Afterward, follow-up decides whether it happens again: about 1 in 5 DKA patients are back within a year. Expect endocrinology within two weeks, and read our sugar emergency guide for the symptom-level detail. Diabetes also raises heart risk, covered on our chest pain page.

911, ER, or Sick-Day Rules?

DKA punishes waiting. Match the response to the symptoms in front of you.

Call 911 Now

Confusion, deep rapid breathing, persistent vomiting, chest pain with diabetes, or a child with diabetes who is suddenly limp or sleepy.

Walk In to the ER

Sugar above 250 with ketones, nausea, or relentless thirst, while you can still keep fluids down. Bring your glucometer and medication list.

Sick-Day Rules at Home

Mild high sugar without ketones: check every 2 to 4 hours, take correction doses, and push fluids. The moment vomiting starts, the plan changes.

DKA Questions, Answered

Can DKA happen if I do not have diabetes?

Yes. DKA is often the first sign of undiagnosed type 1 diabetes, especially in children, teens and young adults. The tell is usually days of weight loss, intense thirst and constant urination before the crisis hits. That pattern deserves a same-day glucose check.

How fast does DKA progress?

It usually builds over about 24 hours, but it can go from mild to severe within 6 to 12 hours, especially once vomiting prevents fluid intake. Do not assume you have more time than you do.

Can I prevent DKA at home with extra insulin?

Sometimes, early. Follow your sick-day rules: check sugar and ketones every 2 to 4 hours, take correction doses, and stay hydrated. Once vomiting starts or ketones keep climbing despite correction, home management is no longer safe and you need IV therapy.

Is DKA fatal?

Treated promptly, rarely: in-hospital mortality runs around 0.4%. The risk climbs with severe episodes, older age, or an underlying infection or heart event, and severe ICU-level cases have been increasing nationally. Speed of treatment is the difference.

What happens after a DKA episode?

Recovery continues after the insulin drip ends. Expect endocrinology follow-up within 1 to 2 weeks, a diabetes-educator session on insulin technique and sick-day rules, and a conversation about continuous glucose monitoring. Addressing the trigger is what prevents the repeat visit.

Does insurance cover ER DKA care?

TL;DR: Kidney stones cause sharp flank or back pain that can radiate to the groin. The pain is often severe and comes in waves. Visit ER of Irving immediately if you have fever, persistent vomiting, blood in urine, a single kidney, or pain you cannot control with oral medication. Our 24/7 emergency facility offers on-site CT, ultrasound, urinalysis, and IV pain and hydration therapy.

What Is a Kidney Stone?

A kidney stone (renal calculus) is a hard mineral deposit that forms inside the kidney when urine becomes concentrated and certain salts crystallize. Small stones often pass on their own. Larger stones can block the ureter, causing severe pain, urinary backup, and infection risk.

According to the NIDDK, about 11% of men and 6% of women in the United States have a kidney stone at least once in their lifetime. The condition is becoming more common, partly because of dietary trends and increasing rates of obesity and diabetes.

Kidney Stone Symptoms You Should Not Ignore

Classic kidney stone symptoms include:

  • Sharp, severe pain in the side or back, just below the ribs
  • Pain that radiates to the lower abdomen and groin
  • Pain that comes in waves and fluctuates in intensity
  • Pink, red, or brown urine (blood in the urine)
  • Cloudy or foul-smelling urine
  • Persistent need to urinate, urinating more often, or burning during urination
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Fever and chills (a sign of possible infection)

Many patients say a kidney stone is the worst pain they have ever felt. Some describe it as worse than childbirth or a broken bone. Pain tends to shift as the stone moves down the urinary tract.

When Kidney Stone Pain Is an ER Emergency

Visit ER of Irving (or call 911) right away if you experience any of the following:

  • Pain so severe that you cannot sit still or find a comfortable position
  • Pain with fever and chills (suggests an infected stone, a true urologic emergency)
  • Pain with persistent vomiting and inability to keep fluids down
  • Blood in the urine paired with severe pain
  • Inability to urinate at all
  • Known history of a single kidney, kidney transplant, or chronic kidney disease
  • Pregnancy combined with suspected stone pain

An infected obstructed kidney can progress to sepsis within hours. Do not wait it out at home.

Types of Kidney Stones

Per the NIDDK, the four main stone types are:

  • Calcium oxalate (the most common, about 80% of stones). Formed when calcium combines with oxalate in concentrated urine.
  • Calcium phosphate. Often linked to metabolic conditions like renal tubular acidosis.
  • Uric acid. Common in people with gout, high-protein diets, or chronic dehydration.
  • Struvite. Forms after a urinary tract infection. Can grow large quickly and cause obstruction.
  • Cystine. Rare, hereditary, and tends to recur from childhood onward.

The treatment plan depends on the type. ER of Irving collects the stone (when possible) for lab analysis so your follow-up urologist can recommend the right prevention strategy.

Why North Texas Climate Increases Kidney Stone Risk

Texas sits in what nephrologists call the "stone belt," a band of southern states with the highest kidney stone rates in the country. Hot summers, sweating, and reduced fluid intake all concentrate urine and accelerate stone formation. Dallas-Fort Worth summers regularly push the heat index past 105 degrees. Staying ahead of dehydration is your single most important prevention step in this climate.

How ER of Irving Diagnoses Kidney Stones

When you arrive with suspected kidney stone pain, our workup typically includes:

  1. Triage and pain control. We do not make you wait in pain for tests. IV pain relief comes early.
  2. Urinalysis. Confirms blood, white cells (suggesting infection), and crystals.
  3. CT scan (low-dose, non-contrast). The diagnostic gold standard for kidney stones. It locates the stone, measures it, and confirms whether the ureter is obstructed.
  4. Ultrasound. First-line for pregnant patients and children to avoid radiation.
  5. Blood work. Checks kidney function and screens for infection.

Most ER stone evaluations are complete within 60 to 90 minutes of arrival.

ER Treatment for Acute Kidney Stones

Treatment depends on stone size, location, and complications.

  • Pain control. NSAIDs (ketorolac) or opioids depending on severity. Pain often improves within 30 minutes.
  • IV fluids. Restore hydration and help flush the stone. See our IV hydration page for what to expect.
  • Anti-nausea medication. For vomiting.
  • Alpha-blocker therapy. Tamsulosin can relax the ureter and help small stones pass.
  • Antibiotics. Started immediately if infection is suspected.
  • Urology referral or transfer. Larger stones (greater than 6 mm) often need lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, or stent placement. We coordinate the next step.

When You Can Manage at Home vs Visit the ER

Symptom ProfileStay Home PlanVisit the ER
Mild flank pain, no fever, can keep fluids downIncrease water, OTC ibuprofen, strain urine for the stoneIf pain becomes unmanageable
Pain with vomitingNot safe at homeYes (we need IV access)
Pain with fever above 101 FNot safe at homeYes (rule out infected stone)
Blood in urine, severe painNot safe at homeYes
Pregnant and suspected stoneNot safe at homeYes (ultrasound, not CT)
One kidney or kidney diseaseNot safe at homeYes (higher complication risk)

Preventing Future Stones

If you have had a stone, your risk of recurrence is about 50% over 10 years. Evidence-based prevention steps include:

  • Drink enough water to produce at least 2 liters of urine per day. In summer, this often means 3 liters of fluid intake.
  • Reduce sodium, which raises urinary calcium.
  • Eat calcium with meals (it binds dietary oxalate in the gut).
  • Limit oxalate-heavy foods (spinach, rhubarb, beets, dark chocolate) if you form calcium oxalate stones.
  • Limit red meat and shellfish if you form uric acid stones.
  • Lemon juice and other citrate sources raise urinary citrate, which inhibits stone formation.

Your urologist may order a 24-hour urine collection to tailor your prevention plan after the acute episode passes.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take a kidney stone to pass?

Stones under 4 mm often pass within 2 weeks. Stones between 4 and 6 mm pass about 60% of the time and may take a month. Stones over 6 mm rarely pass on their own and usually need a procedure.

Can a kidney stone come back after I pass it?

Yes. About half of people who have one stone will have another within 5 to 10 years without prevention measures.

Can I drink coffee or alcohol if I have a stone?

Caffeine and alcohol both dehydrate you, which makes stone passage harder. Stick with water during an active episode.

Is it safe to fly with a kidney stone?

Flying does not cause stones to move, but the pain and vomiting are hard to manage at 30,000 feet. If you have a known stone and severe pain, complete an ER evaluation before traveling.

Will insurance cover an ER kidney stone visit?

TL;DR: A heart attack is a medical emergency. Every 40 seconds, someone in the United States has one. If you feel chest pressure, jaw or arm pain, sudden shortness of breath, cold sweats, or nausea, call 911 immediately. Do not drive yourself. ER of Irving is open 24/7 with on-site EKG, cardiac enzyme labs, and direct cath-lab coordination to keep you inside the "golden hour" window where minutes change outcomes.

What Is a Heart Attack?

A heart attack (myocardial infarction) happens when blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked, usually by a clot in a coronary artery. Without oxygen, that section of muscle starts to die within minutes. The longer the artery stays blocked, the larger the area of permanent damage.

According to the CDC, about 805,000 Americans have a heart attack each year, and roughly 1 in 5 happen silently. The damage is done before the person realizes anything was wrong.

A heart attack is different from a cardiac arrest. A heart attack is a plumbing problem (blocked artery). A cardiac arrest is an electrical problem (the heart stops beating). The two can occur together, and both demand immediate emergency care.

Heart Attack Warning Signs You Should Never Ignore

Classic heart-attack symptoms include:

  • Chest pressure, squeezing, or fullness that lasts more than a few minutes (or goes away and comes back)
  • Pain or discomfort that radiates to the jaw, neck, shoulders, back, or one or both arms
  • Sudden shortness of breath, with or without chest pain
  • Cold sweat, nausea, or lightheadedness
  • A sense of impending doom

The pain does not always feel sharp. Many people describe it as a heavy weight on the chest, like a stack of bricks. The American Heart Association notes that pain at rest, or pain that persists when you stop moving, is a critical red flag.

Compare this to a pulled chest muscle or heartburn, which usually changes with movement, position, or food intake. A heart attack will not improve when you sit still.

Why Heart Attack Symptoms Differ in Women

The American Heart Association reports that women are 30% less likely than men to report chest pain during a heart attack. About 70% of women experience unusual fatigue for days or weeks before the event.

Common heart-attack symptoms in women include:

  • Pain or discomfort in the upper back, jaw, neck, or arms
  • Unusual or unexplained fatigue
  • Shortness of breath
  • Nausea or vomiting
  • Indigestion-like discomfort
  • Sweating with no clear trigger

Because these symptoms feel less classic, women often delay calling 911. They sometimes blame the flu, stress, or heartburn. Treatment delays cost heart muscle.

If you are a woman experiencing two or more of the above symptoms, especially with no clear cause, treat it as a cardiac emergency until a clinician proves otherwise.

The Golden Hour: Why Time Matters Most

ER cardiologists talk about "time is muscle." For every minute a coronary artery stays blocked, more heart cells die. The current American College of Cardiology recommendation is a door-to-balloon time (the interval between hospital arrival and reopening the blocked artery) of 90 minutes or less for an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

That clock starts when you call 911, not when you arrive. Paramedics in the field can run a 12-lead EKG, transmit it ahead, and activate the cath-lab team before you reach the door. Driving yourself wastes those minutes.

ER of Irving is open 24/7 with on-site EKG, troponin and cardiac-enzyme lab testing, and direct coordination with regional cath-lab partners. Our team is trained to identify a STEMI within the first 10 minutes of triage and route you to definitive care immediately.

How ER of Irving Treats a Suspected Heart Attack

When you arrive at ER of Irving with suspected cardiac symptoms, our protocol moves fast:

  1. Triage in under 5 minutes. Vital signs, pulse oximetry, brief history.
  2. 12-lead EKG within 10 minutes. This identifies STEMI (complete artery blockage), non-STEMI, or unstable angina.
  3. Cardiac enzyme labs. Troponin levels confirm if heart muscle is damaged. We use high-sensitivity assays for early detection.
  4. Imaging if indicated. Chest X-ray to rule out aortic dissection or pulmonary embolism, both of which can mimic a heart attack.
  5. Stabilization. Oxygen if saturation is low, aspirin, anti-clotting medication, nitroglycerin, and pain control as appropriate.
  6. Cath-lab activation and transfer. For STEMI, we coordinate immediate transfer to a partner facility for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).

For chest pain that turns out not to be cardiac, we still look for other dangerous causes: pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, pericarditis, or a pulled chest muscle before discharge.

Heart Attack Risk Factors

Per the CDC, the most significant modifiable risk factors include:

  • High blood pressure (hypertension)
  • High LDL cholesterol
  • Smoking or tobacco use
  • Diabetes, especially uncontrolled
  • Obesity
  • Physical inactivity
  • Heavy alcohol use

Non-modifiable risk factors include age (men over 45, women over 55), family history of early heart disease, and certain ethnic backgrounds. About half of Americans have at least one of the three big risks: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or smoking.

Heart Attack vs Heartburn vs Pulled Muscle vs Anxiety

Chest pain has many causes. Knowing the differences can save your life or save you an unnecessary ER trip. Still, when in doubt, choose the ER.

ConditionPain PatternTriggersOther SymptomsAction
Heart attackPressure, squeezing, persistentRest or exertionSweating, nausea, jaw or arm painCall 911
HeartburnBurning, behind breastboneMeals, lying flatSour taste, relief from antacidsTrack, evaluate if severe
Pulled chest muscleSharp, position-dependentMovement, deep breathTender to touch, recent strainRest, NSAIDs
Anxiety attackTight, flutteryStress, panic triggerHyperventilation, tingling in fingersCalm-down, evaluate if recurring
CostochondritisSharp, localizedPressing on ribTender at rib-cartilage junctionOften self-limits
Pulmonary embolismSharp, with breathingRecent surgery, travel, leg swellingSudden shortness of breath, rapid pulseCall 911

For a deeper breakdown of these differentials, see Chest Pain: Muscular, Lung, or Heart?. For the heartburn vs heart attack question specifically, see our Sudden Chest Pressure guide.

When to Call 911 vs Drive to the ER

Call 911, do not drive yourself, if you experience:

  • Chest pressure or pain lasting more than 5 minutes
  • Pain spreading to jaw, arm, neck, or back
  • Sudden shortness of breath
  • Cold sweat with chest discomfort
  • Fainting, collapse, or sudden severe weakness
  • Heart-attack symptoms in someone over 50 with known cardiac risk

EMS can begin oxygen and aspirin in the ambulance, transmit your EKG to the cath-lab team, and bypass the triage line. You arrive faster and better.

Drive to ER of Irving only if symptoms are mild and stable, you are not alone, and the trip is shorter than 10 minutes. Even then, have someone else drive you.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a heart attack feel like indigestion?

Yes. Some heart attacks present primarily as upper-abdominal burning, especially in women and people with diabetes. If the burning is new, severe, or paired with sweating, treat it as cardiac until proven otherwise.

How long does a heart attack last?

Symptoms can last from a few minutes to several hours. Even brief, repeated episodes (so-called angina) signal coronary artery disease and warrant urgent evaluation.

Can a young person have a heart attack?

Yes. Coronary spasm, drug use (including stimulant medications), spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), and genetic high cholesterol all cause heart attacks in younger adults. Symptoms should never be dismissed because of age.

What happens after a heart attack?

Patients typically transfer from ER of Irving to a hospital with a cardiac cath lab for PCI or, in some cases, surgery. Long-term care includes cardiac rehabilitation, medications, and lifestyle changes.

Will my insurance cover this?

Per the federal No Surprises Act and Texas Department of Insurance balance-billing rules, patients are protected from balance billing for emergency care. We post all required disclosures under Texas H&S Code Chapter 254 and can discuss costs with you on arrival.

Visit ER of Irving for 24/7 Cardiac Emergency Care

Heart attacks do not wait for office hours. ER of Irving is open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, with no appointment required and minimal wait times. Our facility is staffed by board-certified emergency physicians, equipped with on-site EKG, lab, and imaging, and connected to regional cath-lab partners for the next step in cardiac care.

If you or someone near you is having heart-attack symptoms, call 911 first. If symptoms are mild and stable, walk in to ER of Irving immediately. For non-emergency questions, see our Chest Pain Treatment service page or Contact Us form. When every minute counts, we are here.

Chest pressure past 5 minutes, pain spreading to jaw or arm, cold sweat, fainting, or sudden breathlessness. EMS starts care in your driveway.

Come to the ER

Mild, stable symptoms, someone else driving, and a trip under 10 minutes. We are open 24/7 with no appointment.

When in Doubt, Choose Us

Heartburn changes with meals. A pulled muscle hurts with movement. A heart attack persists at rest. If you cannot tell, let the EKG decide.

Heart Attack Questions, Answered

Can a heart attack feel like indigestion?

Yes. Some heart attacks present mainly as upper-abdominal burning, especially in women and people with diabetes. If the burning is new, severe, or paired with sweating or breathlessness, treat it as cardiac until an EKG and labs prove otherwise.

How long does a heart attack last?

Symptoms can run from a few minutes to several hours. Even brief, repeated episodes that ease with rest signal coronary artery disease and deserve urgent evaluation. Do not wait for pain to become constant before acting.

Can a young person have a heart attack?

Yes. Coronary artery spasm, stimulant use, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, and inherited high cholesterol all cause heart attacks in younger adults. Age alone is never a reason to dismiss classic symptoms.

Who is most at risk for a heart attack?

High blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, obesity, and inactivity drive most risk, and about half of Americans have at least one of the big three. Age, family history of early heart disease, and menopause add non-modifiable risk.

What happens after a heart attack?

Patients are stabilized here, then transferred to a cath-lab facility where cardiologists reopen the artery, usually with a stent. Recovery includes cardiac rehabilitation, medications, and follow-up with a cardiologist. Many people return to full, active lives.

Will my insurance cover emergency heart attack care?

Emergency care is protected. Under the federal No Surprises Act and Texas Department of Insurance balance-billing rules, patients are shielded from surprise balance bills for emergency treatment. We post all required Texas disclosures and can discuss costs with you on arrival.

When Every Minute Counts, We Are Here

Call 911 first for heart attack signs. For mild, stable symptoms, walk in any time. Experienced emergency physicians, EKG, labs and imaging, 24 hours a day.

Understanding Chest Pain: Common Causes

Chest pain can arise from various conditions, some of which require urgent medical intervention. At ER of Irving, we assess and treat all causes, including:

Heart Attack (Myocardial infarction): severe, crushing pain, often accompanied by sweating, nausea, and shortness of breath

Angina: chest discomfort due to reduced blood flow to the heart

Pericarditis: inflammation of the lining around the heart, causing sharp chest pain

Aortic Dissection: A life-threatening condition requiring immediate medical intervention

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD): acid reflux causing burning pain

Pulmonary Embolism (PE): A blood clot in the lungs, leading to sharp pain and difficulty breathing

Musculoskeletal Pain: Strained muscles, costochondritis, or rib fractures
