The workup follows the danger list in order. An EKG catches heart attacks in progress. Troponin blood testing catches the ones an EKG can miss. How do I know if chest pain is a heart attack or heartburn?

You often cannot tell from symptoms alone, and neither can a doctor without testing. Heart attack pain tends toward pressure and squeezing, spreads to the arm or jaw, and comes with sweating or breathlessness. Heartburn burns and worsens lying down. When in doubt, get an EKG. It takes minutes.

Should I call 911 or drive to the ER for chest pain?

An EKG within minutes of arrival, troponin blood testing that detects heart muscle injury, and chest imaging when the lungs need checking. All run on-site, 24/7, with results the same visit. Together they rule a heart attack in or out with high confidence.

Are heart attack symptoms different for women?

Often, yes. Women more frequently experience unusual fatigue, nausea, jaw or back pain, and breathlessness rather than crushing chest pressure. Those quieter symptoms are heart attacks just as often, which is why unexplained upper-body discomfort in women deserves the same urgent workup.

BE-FAST: The Stroke Signs to Know

Any one of these, appearing suddenly, is a stroke until proven otherwise.

B: Balance Lost

Sudden dizziness, stumbling, or loss of coordination.

E: Eyes Failing

Sudden blurred, double, or lost vision in one or both eyes.

F: Face Drooping

One side of the smile sags. Ask the person to smile and compare.

A: Arm Weakness

One arm drifts down when both are raised, or grip suddenly weakens.

S: Speech Trouble

Slurred words, wrong words, or trouble understanding simple sentences.

T: Time to Call 911

Note when symptoms started and call 911 immediately. Do not drive.

Symptoms That Pass

A TIA warns a major stroke may follow within days. Still an emergency.

A sudden thunderclap headache can signal bleeding in the brain.

A transient ischemic attack: stroke symptoms that resolve on their own, usually within minutes. It means a clot briefly blocked blood flow, and a major stroke often follows within days. Even if you feel fine now, come in the same day for a workup.

What Is a Traumatic Brain Injury?

A traumatic brain injury is damage to the brain caused by a sudden blow, jolt, or penetrating injury to the head. Severity ranges from mild concussions to life-threatening bleeding and swelling inside the skull. The CDC reports roughly 2.4 million emergency department visits each year involve a TBI, with falls and motor-vehicle crashes the two leading causes.

Symptoms do not always appear right away. Bleeding inside the skull can worsen for hours while a person feels fine. That is why prompt evaluation after any significant head impact matters, even without visible injury.

TBI Warning Signs That Need the ER Now

Loss of Consciousness

Any blackout after impact, even a brief one, needs same-day evaluation.

Worsening Headache

A headache that builds instead of fading can signal bleeding or swelling.

Repeated Vomiting

More than one episode of vomiting after head trauma is a red flag.

Slurred Speech or Confusion

Trouble speaking, recognizing people, or answering questions needs urgent assessment.

Unequal Pupils or Vision Changes

One pupil larger than the other or blurred vision after impact.

Seizures

Any convulsion after a head injury requires emergency care.

Clear Fluid From Nose or Ears

Leaking clear fluid can indicate a skull fracture.

Loss of Balance

New dizziness, stumbling, or weakness on one side of the body.

How We Diagnose and Treat TBI

Our emergency team follows a clear process the moment you arrive. A physician examines you, checks neurological function, and orders CT imaging on-site when indicated. Results come back fast because everything happens under one roof.

Treatment depends on severity. Mild TBI and concussions are managed with observation, symptom control, and clear return-to-activity guidance. Go to the ER

Loss of consciousness, vomiting, confusion, seizures, or any blood-thinner use. We have CT imaging.

Urgent Care Works

Minor scalp cuts with no impact symptoms and no loss of consciousness.

Lingering mild symptoms days after an injury already evaluated in an ER.

When should I go to the ER after hitting my head?

Go immediately if you lost consciousness, vomit more than once, feel confused, have a worsening headache, or take blood thinners. Symptoms can appear hours after impact, so err on the side of evaluation. ER of Irving is open 24/7 with no appointment needed.

What happens if my TBI is severe?

We stabilize you first. Our team manages airway, breathing, and pressure on the brain, then coordinates rapid transfer to a trauma center or neurosurgical service when advanced care is needed. The receiving team gets your imaging and records directly from us.

A Concussion Is a Brain Injury, Not a Bruise

A concussion changes how the brain works for days to weeks, even when scans look normal. According to the CDC’s HEADS UP program, the biggest risk is going back to sports or full activity before the brain has healed, when a second hit does far more damage than the first.

The advice has also changed. Days alone in a dark room is outdated; recovery now means a short period of rest followed by a gradual, symptom-guided return.

Our emergency room in Irving does the evaluation the same day: a full neurological exam, a CT scan only when red flags call for one, and a written plan for the weeks ahead.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: July 2026

Concussion Symptoms to Take Seriously

The first two mean call 911, because they can signal a bleed rather than a concussion. The rest deserve a same-day exam.

Symptoms Getting Worse

A headache that builds, repeated vomiting, or growing confusion can mean a bleed. Call 911.

One Pupil Larger

Unequal pupils, a seizure, or someone you cannot wake are 911 emergencies.

Headache and Pressure

The most common symptom, often with sensitivity to light and noise.

Fog and Slow Thinking

Feeling off, answering slowly, or struggling to focus at school or work.

Dizziness and Balance Trouble

The room spins, or walking a straight line suddenly takes effort.

Nausea Right After the Hit

Queasiness in the first hours is common. Repeated vomiting is not.

Sleep That Changes

Sleeping far more than usual, or unable to fall asleep at all.

Mood Swings

Irritability, anxiety, or tears that are out of character, especially in teens.

What Happens the Moment You Arrive

Concussion care is an exam-first visit. Most people are in and out with a plan in about an hour.

1. Same-Day Evaluation

A physician exam within minutes: memory, balance, eye movement, and reaction.

2. CT Only If Needed

Red flags earn a scan to rule out a bleed. A typical concussion does not need radiation.

3. A Real Recovery Plan

Written instructions for rest, screens, school or work, and a stepwise return to activity.

4. Return-to-Play Guidance

Athletes leave with the graduated protocol schools and coaches expect.

How Concussion Recovery Actually Works

The first 24 to 48 hours are for taking it easy: less screen time, no sports, lighter mental load. After that, activity comes back step by step, with symptoms setting the pace. Most people recover fully within two to four weeks.

Children and teens heal on a slower clock and need a doctor’s clearance before returning to play. Our pediatric emergency team walks families through the school and sports timeline.

If symptoms suddenly worsen during recovery, that is no longer concussion territory. Head to our head injury emergency care page for the red flags, and come in immediately if any appear.

911, ER, or Rest at Home?

The second hit before healing is the dangerous one. Here is how to pace it.

Call 911 Now

Worsening confusion, repeated vomiting, a seizure, unequal pupils, or someone you cannot wake. Do not drive them.

Get Checked Today

Any suspected concussion deserves a same-day exam, especially a student athlete who wants a safe return to play.

Recover at Home

After a clean evaluation: 24 to 48 hours of taking it easy, then a gradual return guided by symptoms.

Concussion Questions, Answered

What will they do for a concussion?

The physician runs a neurological exam covering memory, balance, eye movement and reaction time, and orders a CT scan only if red flags suggest bleeding. You go home with a written recovery plan: what to rest, when to return to school or work, and exactly which symptoms mean come back.

Do I need to go to the ER for a concussion?

A same-day evaluation is worth it every time. It rules out the dangerous look-alikes, documents a baseline, and replaces guesswork with a plan. Go immediately if symptoms worsen, vomiting repeats, or the person is confused, hard to wake, or has unequal pupils.

How long does a concussion take to heal?

Most adults recover fully within two to four weeks. Children and teens often need longer, and pushing through symptoms stretches the timeline instead of shortening it. Symptoms lasting beyond a month deserve a follow-up visit rather than more waiting.

Can my child return to sports after a concussion?

Yes, but never the same day, and never without medical clearance. Texas schools follow a graduated return-to-play protocol: light activity first, then sport-specific drills, then contact, with each step earned symptom-free. We provide the evaluation and documentation that process requires.

Is it safe to sleep after a concussion?

Yes. After a clean evaluation, sleep actually helps the brain recover, and the old advice to wake someone every hour is outdated. The exception is before evaluation: if the person is unusually hard to wake or confused when woken, that is an emergency.

Recover Right the First Time

Second hits before healing are the dangerous ones. Get evaluated today, walk out with a plan, and return with confidence.

Get Directions

Why a Hard Hit to the Head Deserves a Look

Most bumps on the head heal with an ice pack. The problem is the exception: slow bleeding inside the skull that can feel like nothing for hours, then turn dangerous fast. According to the CDC, people can seem fine after a serious head injury and decline later the same day.

Risk climbs with age, with blood thinners, and with any hit hard enough to cause confusion or memory gaps. From the outside, a concussion and a bleed can look identical.

Our emergency room in Irving settles it with a CT scan on-site, read in minutes. You leave knowing what happened inside, not guessing.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: July 2026

Head Injury Signs That Need the ER Now

The first two mean call 911. For the rest, come straight in. A CT scan settles it either way.

Unconscious or Hard to Wake

If they passed out and stay confused, or you cannot keep them awake, call 911.

Seizure After the Hit

A seizure following any head injury is a 911 emergency. Keep them safe and call.

Vomiting More Than Once

Repeated vomiting after a head hit points to pressure building inside the skull.

A Worsening Headache

Pain that builds instead of fading, especially hours after the injury.

Confusion or Odd Behavior

Slurred speech, repeated questions, or simply not acting like themselves.

Unequal Pupils or Blurred Vision

One pupil larger than the other, double vision, or trouble focusing.

On Blood Thinners

Any head hit while taking blood thinners deserves a CT scan, even if you feel fine.

Fluid From Nose or Ears

Clear or bloody fluid leaking after a head hit can mean a skull fracture.

What Happens the Moment You Arrive

Head injuries skip the waiting room. The exam starts with alertness, memory, and pupils.

1. Straight Back

A physician checks alertness, pupils, and memory within minutes of arrival.

2. Neuro Exam

Balance, reflexes, vision, and the story of exactly how the hit happened.

3. CT Scan On-Site

The scan that rules a bleed in or out takes minutes, with results read right away.

4. Observe, Treat, or Transfer

Most people go home with a clear plan. Bleeds are stabilized and transferred to neurosurgery.

How We Treat Head Injuries

The CT scan drives everything. A clean scan with concussion symptoms means rest instructions, a recovery plan, and our concussion care pathway for the days that follow. A bleed means stabilization here and rapid transfer to a neurosurgical team.

Serious injuries run through our traumatic brain injury protocol, with repeat neuro checks to catch any change early.

Kids fall constantly, and most are fine. Our pediatric emergency team examines children gently and uses CT only when the exam truly calls for it, keeping radiation exposure as low as possible.

911, ER, or Watch at Home?

The hit itself matters less than what happens in the hours after it.

Call 911 Now

Unconscious, a seizure, repeated vomiting with drowsiness, or one pupil bigger than the other. Do not drive them.

Come to the ER

Confusion, a worsening headache, vision changes, a fall in someone over 65, or any hit while on blood thinners.

Watch at Home

A light bump with no symptoms, where the person stays alert and acts normally, can be watched for 24 hours.

Head Injury Questions, Answered

When should I go to the ER after hitting my head?

Go if there was any loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, vision changes, or memory gaps. Go regardless of symptoms if you take blood thinners or are over 65. A hit hard enough to make you wonder is a hit worth checking.

What does head injury treatment involve?

It starts with a neurological exam and a CT scan to rule out bleeding inside the skull. A clean scan with concussion symptoms means structured rest and a recovery plan. A bleed means stabilization and rapid transfer to neurosurgery. Both paths start with knowing, not guessing.

Is it a concussion or something worse?

You cannot reliably tell from the outside. A concussion is a functional injury that recovers with rest, while a brain bleed is structural and worsens with time. Early symptoms overlap almost completely, which is exactly what the CT scan is for.

My child hit their head. What should I watch for?

Come in for vomiting, unusual sleepiness, a worsening headache, confusion, or any behavior that is not your child’s normal. For a light bump where they cry briefly and return to playing, watch them closely for 24 hours. When in doubt, bring them in.

Can a head injury be treated at home?

A minor bump with no warning signs can be managed with ice, rest, and watching for changes over 24 hours. Home care is never right when there was loss of consciousness, vomiting, confusion, or blood thinner use. Those need a CT scan first, then rest.

The Bleed You Cannot See Is the One That Matters

If the hit was hard enough to make you wonder, that is reason enough. Walk in any time for a CT scan and a real answer.

Understanding Breathing Problems and Their Causes

Breathing problems can stem from a variety of conditions, ranging from mild to severe. It’s important to understand the underlying causes of these issues so that appropriate treatment can be provided. Common causes of breathing difficulties include:

  • Asthma: A chronic condition that causes inflammation and narrowing of the airways, making it difficult to breathe.
  • Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): A progressive lung disease that obstructs airflow and causes breathing difficulties.
  • Pneumonia: An infection in the lungs that causes inflammation and fluid buildup, leading to breathing problems.
  • Anaphylaxis: A severe allergic reaction that can cause the throat to swell, restricting airflow.
  • Heart Failure: A condition where the heart is unable to pump blood effectively, leading to fluid buildup in the lungs and difficulty breathing.
  • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): A severe condition where the lungs cannot provide enough oxygen to the body due to inflammation.

If you are experiencing any of these symptoms, it’s crucial to seek emergency respiratory care immediately to prevent the situation from worsening.

A fracture is a break in the bone, and a bad sprain can feel exactly like one. According to MedlinePlus, imaging is the only reliable way to tell them apart. Guessing wrong means walking on a break for days and risking a bone that heals crooked.

Treatment depends on the break. Simple fractures get a splint or cast and heal on their own. Displaced bones may need a closed reduction, where the physician realigns the bone under pain medication before splinting.

Every fracture visit starts with on-site digital X-ray or CT to map the break exactly. For children, our pediatric emergency team pays special attention to growth plates.

Complex breaks that need surgery are stabilized here first, then referred to an orthopedic surgeon with imaging already done. You leave with the bone protected, pain controlled, and a clear plan.

How can I tell if a bone is broken or just sprained?

You usually cannot tell without an X-ray. A snap at the moment of injury, visible deformity, and inability to bear weight all point to a break, but a bad sprain can swell and hurt just as much. Imaging is the only reliable answer.

Most do not. Simple breaks heal in a cast or splint over several weeks. Surgery is usually reserved for bones broken in several places, breaks that will not stay aligned, or fractures through a joint. Imaging tells us which kind yours is, and we arrange the referral if needed.

Cleaners, solvents, or industrial chemicals in the eye. Rinse and come in immediately.

Metal shavings, glass, sand, or debris that will not flush out.

Sharp pain, tearing, and light sensitivity after a scratch or poke.

Any object that has pierced the eye. Shield it, do not remove it.

Vision that dims, blurs, or disappears in one or both eyes.

Swelling, discharge, and pain, including severe pink eye that is getting worse.

Four steps, one roof, no appointment.

What you do in the first minutes matters. For chemical splashes, rinse the open eye with clean water for a full 15 minutes before heading in. For everything else, the rule is simpler: do not rub the eye, do not try to remove an embedded object, and do not apply pressure.

If an object is sticking out of the eye, cover it loosely with a rigid shield, even the bottom of a paper cup taped in place, and come straight to the ER. Keep both eyes closed as much as possible, since they move together.

Not every eye problem needs an ER. Here is how to choose fast.

Come to the ER

Injuries, chemical splashes, sudden vision loss, severe pain, or infection with fever. Open 24/7.

Flashes, new floaters, or a curtain over your vision. Retinal problems are time-critical.

Can an ER treat eye injuries?

What should I do if something is stuck in my eye?

Do not rub the eye or try to pull the object out. Blink gently to let tears flush small debris. If it does not clear, or the object is embedded, cover the eye loosely and come to the ER immediately.

What is the first aid for chemicals in the eye?

Rinse immediately. Hold the eye open under clean running water for a full 15 minutes, then come straight to the ER. Bring the chemical container or its name if you can. Fast rinsing is the single biggest factor in saving vision after a splash.

Should I go to the ER for pink eye?

Most pink eye can wait for a regular doctor. Come to the ER if you have severe pain, vision changes, intense light sensitivity, fever, or symptoms that worsen quickly. Those signs can point to a deeper infection that needs immediate treatment.

Is sudden vision loss an emergency?

Yes, always. Vision that suddenly dims, blurs, or disappears can signal retinal detachment, blocked blood flow, or another time-critical problem. Come to the ER immediately, even if the vision loss is painless or seems to improve on its own.

The CDC estimates 48 million Americans get a foodborne illness each year, and about 128,000 end up hospitalized. Most cases pass in a day or two with rest and fluids. Mono gets confirmed so you stop wondering why the fatigue will not lift. Viral sore throats get honest guidance and real symptom relief instead of antibiotics that would not help.

Any warning sign above, suspected strep needing a test, or a child who stops drinking.

Sore Throat Treatment Questions, Answered

How do I know if my sore throat is strep?

You cannot tell by looking, and neither can a doctor with certainty. Strep tends to bring sudden throat pain, fever, and swollen tonsils without a cough, but the only reliable answer is a rapid strep test. Ours returns results in minutes, any hour of the day.

When is a sore throat an emergency?

When breathing or swallowing is affected. Trouble breathing, drooling, inability to swallow saliva, a muffled voice, or severe one-sided pain can mean an abscess or airway swelling. Those need immediate care, not a next-day appointment.

Do you test for strep and mono on-site?

Yes. Rapid strep and mono testing run in our on-site lab 24/7, with results in minutes. If strep is positive, antibiotics start the same visit. If mono is confirmed, you leave knowing what is causing the fatigue and how to recover safely.

Does strep throat need antibiotics?

Yes, once a test confirms it. Antibiotics shorten the illness, cut the contagious window to about 24 hours, and prevent rare complications like rheumatic fever. Viral sore throats, which are the majority, do not benefit from antibiotics at all.

When a Digestive Problem Becomes an Emergency

Digestive diseases affect an estimated 60 to 70 million Americans, according to the NIH NIDDK. Most are managed over time with a doctor. The emergencies are different: internal bleeding, a blocked bowel, a gallbladder attack, or severe constipation that has become an impaction. Those escalate in hours, not weeks.

The tell is usually a sudden change: abdominal pain that sharpens, vomiting that will not stop, or a bathroom pattern that halts completely. When your gut changes its behavior abruptly, that deserves imaging, not another day of waiting.

Medically reviewed by the ER of Irving Medical Team | Updated: July 2026

GI Warning Signs That Need the ER Now

Come in immediately if you notice any of these.

Blood in Stool or Vomit

Red blood, coffee-ground vomit, or black tarry stools mean internal bleeding.

Bowel Obstruction Signs

No stool or gas, swollen belly, cramping waves, and vomiting.

Severe Constipation

Days without a bowel movement plus pain, bloating, or vomiting.

Gallbladder Attack

Upper right pain after fatty meals, radiating to the back or shoulder.

Ulcer Pain That Worsens

Burning pain that intensifies or comes with dizziness or dark stools.

Fever With Belly Pain

Can signal diverticulitis or another infection needing treatment now.

Vomiting That Will Not Stop

Especially green bile or anything resembling coffee grounds.

Rapid Unexplained Changes

Sudden weight loss or swallowing trouble deserves same-day answers.

What to Expect When You Arrive

Four steps, one roof, no appointment.

1. Walk In

Check-in takes minutes. Median door-to-provider time is under 10 minutes.

2. Physician Exam

An emergency physician examines your abdomen and reviews your history.

3. CT and Labs On-Site

Imaging finds obstructions, stones, and inflammation the same visit.

4. Treatment and Referral

Relief starts here, with GI specialist coordination when ongoing care is needed.

GI Conditions We Treat Around the Clock

We handle the acute side of digestive disease: GI bleeding, bowel obstructions, fecal impaction, gallbladder and gallstone attacks, diverticulitis flares, severe acid reflux and ulcer complications, and pancreatitis. CT imaging and full lab work run on-site, so the diagnosis lands the same visit, and treatment, from IV fluids and pain control to antibiotics, starts before you leave.

When the emergency overlaps with something you ate, our food poisoning workup covers it. When surgery or a scope is needed, we stabilize you and coordinate directly with the right specialist, records in hand.

ER or GI Specialist? An Honest Guide

Both have a role. Here is how to pick tonight.

Come to the ER

Bleeding, obstruction signs, severe pain, or any warning card above. We rule out the dangerous causes tonight.

See a GI Specialist

Chronic reflux, IBS management, screening colonoscopies, and long-term condition care.

Do Not Wait On

Black stools, a belly that stops moving, or pain that keeps climbing. Hours matter.

GI Emergency Questions, Answered

When should you go to the hospital for constipation?

When days without a bowel movement come with belly pain, bloating, vomiting, or the inability to pass gas. That combination can mean fecal impaction or a bowel obstruction, both of which need imaging and treatment rather than another laxative at home.

What are the symptoms of a bowel obstruction?

Cramping waves of belly pain, a swollen abdomen, vomiting, and no stool or gas passing. Symptoms often build over hours. An obstruction can cut off blood flow to the bowel, so these signs need a CT scan the same day, not a wait-and-see approach.

Is blood in the stool an emergency?

Treat it as one until proven otherwise. Bright red blood, black tarry stools, or coffee-ground vomit all point to bleeding somewhere in the digestive tract. We check blood counts and vital signs immediately and find the source before it becomes dangerous.

What does a gallbladder attack feel like?

Intense pain in the upper right belly, often after a fatty meal, sometimes radiating to the right shoulder or back, with nausea. Attacks that last more than a few hours, or come with fever or yellowing skin, need same-day evaluation and imaging.

Emergency Care Questions, Answered

Is ER of Irving a real emergency room?

Yes. We are a Texas-licensed freestanding emergency medical care facility with board-certified emergency physicians, on-site CT, X-ray, ultrasound and laboratory, open 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. We treat the same emergencies a hospital emergency department treats, and we coordinate direct transfer when surgery or ICU admission is needed.

Do I need an appointment?

No. Emergency care is walk-in by nature. Come in any hour of any day, including weekends and holidays. Our median door-to-provider time is under 10 minutes.

Should I go to the ER or urgent care?

Urgent care fits minor illness during business hours: a mild cold, a small cut, a routine sprain. Anything involving chest pain, breathing trouble, stroke signs, severe pain, head injury, or a child under 3 months with a fever belongs in an emergency room. When in doubt, call us at (972) 893-3148 and ask.

Will my insurance cover the visit?

Emergency care is protected. Under the federal No Surprises Act and Texas Department of Insurance balance-billing rules, patients are shielded from surprise balance bills for emergency treatment. We accept most major insurance and post all required Texas disclosures.

Do you treat children?

Yes. We evaluate and treat pediatric emergencies with age-appropriate equipment, and when a child needs subspecialty care we coordinate direct transfer to Children’s Health Dallas or Cook Children’s in Fort Worth.

What if I need surgery or hospital admission?

We stabilize you first, complete the workup, and arrange direct transfer to the right hospital with your imaging and records already done. That head start often shortens the total time to definitive treatment.
